payload.acceptance_criteria:
- When installed with either distribution, tracker-owned vault clones shall receive the same push guard automatically.
- When a protected clone pushes, the guard shall validate every outgoing commit and ref update.
- When a push changes unexpected paths or invalid events, it shall refuse before remote history changes.
- When a push deletes or rewrites history, creates another branch, or pushes tags, it shall refuse.
- When tracker batches are valid, normal concurrent sharing and retries shall still succeed.
- When protection is requested for an existing vault clone, installation shall preserve unrelated hooks or refuse without changes.
- When installed or updated, protection shall remain usable on Windows, Linux, and macOS without another hook dependency.
- When pushed through the tracker, validation shall run without disabling hooks.
- When a code repository pushes ordinary code, vault-specific restrictions shall not apply.
- When installation or validation fails, queued events and existing repository files shall remain intact.
- When a manually cloned vault lacks protection, guidance shall name the explicit protection command.
payload.description:
## Context

The owner wants accidental agent and human pushes rejected before they add unrelated files to backlog-vault.
The standalone tracker and basicly must install and maintain protection with little setup.
Existing commit quarantine only controls accepted tracker history after a push.
It does not prevent unwanted Git objects or refs from reaching the remote.
Current vault_share._push also selects an empty hooks directory.
Replace that override with the reviewed tracker guard rather than bypassing protection.

## Scope

- Tracker kit push validation and hook installation.
- Automatic protection for tracker-owned clones and explicit protection for manual clones.
- Standalone and harness guidance and cross-platform consumer checks.

## Plan

- demonstration: `uv run pytest tests/test_kit_vault_push_guard.py tests/test_kit_vault_push_guard_consumer.py tests/test_kit_vault_share.py tests/test_kit_vault_cli_wiring.py -q` proves valid sharing and refused malformed pushes against fixture remotes.
payload.requirements: Share one validator and installer across standalone and harness distributions. Use Git native hooks and the existing Python runtime. Add no dependency. Never modify global Git configuration. Preserve caller-owned hooks and repository files. Demonstrate refusal with unchanged actual remote refs. Local hooks prevent accidents; deliberately bypassed hooks and server policy enforcement are separate boundaries. Remote settings need separate owner approval.
payload.title: Reject accidental non-tracker pushes from vault clones

payload.text:
[design note 2026-11-16, basicly session, no code] Burst margin: two protocol options

Measured baseline (Trace2 plus a span profiler on the unchanged test; deadline, clone count, latency and workers unchanged):
- The last publisher in line needs 13 push rounds. The injected floor is 13 x 1.5 s = 19.5 s.
- Per round it also waits 0.3-0.45 s for a fetch. That fetch already started before the rejection in 86 of 91 matched waits.
- Real push: 0.045 s alone, 0.24 s in the full suite on 4 CPUs, 0.49 s on 2 CPUs. On 2 CPUs the pre-push guard process is 0.39 s of it.
- One failing 2-CPU run started 5183 Git processes in 30 s. The 39 joiner threads made 297 of the 312 fetches.
- Slowest publisher: 27.1-29.65 s when passing, 29.9 s when failing. The smallest margin seen in a pass is 0.35 s.
- No single wasted step reached 5 s, so this is a protocol question and not a hotfix.

Option 1: joiners stop fetching; the publisher fetches once per round, during its push.
- Change: a joining session waits on the share lock holder's progress file instead of running its own helper refresh. The publisher starts one fetch beside each push, so the retry overlap stays.
- Expected gain: 0.5 to 3 s on 2 CPUs, about 0 to 1 s on 4 CPUs (assumed). Basis: about 60 % of runner calls and 95 % of fetches come from joiners. Real push time scales with load (0.24 s at 4 CPUs, 0.49 s at 2 CPUs). The gain assumes queue time falls with process count, which is not measured. It can lose up to 1.8 s if the publisher fetch overlaps less than the joiner fetches do now.
- Size: 6 to 10 hours (assumed), including the join-path tests.
- Risk: the takeover and joined-claim paths depend on joiner refresh (test_a_live_sharer_finishes_after_takeover..., test_a_joined_claim_reserves_time...).

Option 2: one ref per writer, so publishers stop competing for main.
- Change: each clone pushes its batch to its own ref, so a push is never rejected. A deterministic fold orders competing claims, for example by the first canonical event. The push guard accepts the writer ref instead of refusing other branches.
- Expected gain: about 15 to 18 s. Basis: 13 rounds become 1, so the injected cost per publisher falls from 19.5 s to 1.5 s, and the retry waits (4 to 5 s) go away.
- Size: 3 to 5 days (assumed). It is a vault protocol change: claim ordering semantics, guard rules, migration of existing vaults, and the old-kit compatibility that basicly-wecjejf tracks.
- Risk: this is a new protocol after release. It conflicts with the frozen 0.46 vault format and needs an owner decision on scope.

Proof that is not luck, for either option:
- Run the unchanged burst test 30 times in each of three conditions: alone on 4 CPUs, the full suite on 4 CPUs, and the vault files with -n 4 on 2 CPUs.
- Record the slowest publisher span of every run, not the pass count.
- Accept only when the minimum margin (30 s minus the slowest span) is at least 5 s in every condition, and the median moves by more than the run-to-run spread of the baseline.
- Measure the baseline distribution first under the same three conditions. Today's smallest passing margin is 0.35 s.

payload.description:
## Context
The owner approved session plan v6 on 2026-11-10 after a five-round hill-climb and three council votes. The plan adapts basicly to the Claude 5 family: model roles, a model table from models.dev, an instruction trim and quiet hook output. The work runs outside basicly loop. The verified facts the plan rests on are on the research record that child A files.

# Session plan v6 for basicly (2026-11-10), final

Repository: the repository root. The owner's request, the standing constraints and all verified facts are in `facts.md` beside this file (read it first). This file is the plan only.

Change from v5 (round 5 fixes, not graded): the trim starts from the cause of each skill read, because the trigger words it planned to add are already in the fragments. Quiet hook output starts with a 5 minute probe, because the Lefthook file is rendered by Python code and its output setting may not reach the followed command. The goal lines say what counts as not met. The Fable reference run is dropped.

## Where we are

- Last session (2026-11-07): plan v4 milestones M0 and M1 shipped as v0.43.0: the skills swarm, council and hill-climb, and all 29 catalog skills at the skill standard. Then the README and the landing page were rewritten. CI on main is green at b8331e2a.
- Backlog: 447 open records, 4 ready. Plan v4 names M2b (fast commit lane) next, then M3 to M8.
- New inputs today: the Claude 5 family with Fable 5.2, Anthropic's cost measurements (facts.md), a measured commit time of 7.2 s, and a transcript analysis of the value pilot.
- This work runs outside `basicly loop`, as the owner asked: the loop is part of what is being rebuilt. The tracker and the commit hooks stay on, with no bypass.

## Goal

By the end of this session:

1. basicly states the role of each model in one place, and a gate enforces what a gate can. Opus 5.5 owns a task. Delegated work names a tier. Fable 5.2 has two written roles: advisor for a hard problem, and orchestrator for work larger than one context window. Every agent a review skill starts has a tier, from its definition or from the repository default. An untiered `general-purpose` start takes the worker tier wherever a repository sets the default-tier variable; this repository sets it.
2. The owner has a table, read from models.dev today, of the newest model per tier and surface and of each stale anchor in the model map.
3. The catalog instruction fragments no longer send every task to a skill, shown by counts from one pilot run before and after (skill files read, model calls, instruction tokens per call). A passing commit prints a short summary in place of 10,220 bytes, measured in bytes on a real commit. If the pinned Lefthook cannot do this or the step is cut, this half is reported as not met and a record holds the finding.
4. Each shipped artifact has been used once in this session, with the output recorded. If the running session does not reload the hook, this line is reported as not met for the hook, and the probe is the first step of the next session. The orchestrator role is used by this session itself. The advisor role cannot be used here, because a Fable session accepts only Fable as advisor; its first use is one `/advisor fable` consult in the next session on Opus 5.5, recorded with its call count.

## Decisions taken (source in brackets)

| Decision | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Default session shape | Opus 5.5 owner; Sonnet 5.5 for delegated work; Haiku 5.5 only to run test suites, never to write tests [council, 2 of 3 counted] |
| Fable 5.2 roles | Advisor on demand (`/advisor fable`); orchestrator as the session model for work larger than one context window; never a delegated worker [owner statement; vendor criterion] |
| `maximum` tier | No catalog agent declares it; `architect` moves to `high` [council, 2 of 3 counted] |
| Advisor configuration | basicly projects nothing; the rule says when to ask [5 of 5 round-1 reviewers; vendor: +1.7 points for 2.1 times the cost, measured with Fable 5.1] |
| Rest of the session | Trim of the instruction fragments [second council vote 2 of 3], plus quiet hook output, which the dissenting voter named as the surer gain and a later commit count supports |
| Model map | Probe models.dev today; the owner decides on regeneration from the table [owner, 2026-11-10]. Answer to the owner's question: deferring the regeneration was right for Claude Code sessions, because the hook writes aliases and the aliases already reach the 5.5 and 5.2 models; it is not established for the Copilot surface, which takes full ids from the map, and the probe settles that |
| Consumers and `maximum` | No new check. `maximum` stays a valid tier for a consumer; the roles rule explains it. A warning channel does not exist in `agents-check`, and a refusal would break an upgrade |

## Where each part of the owner's request goes

- Artifact order "agent instructions, skills, work tracker, work loop": today is agent instructions (the roles rule, the trimmed fragments) and the tiers inside the review skills. Step A comes before the instruction trim only because the trim runs during the CI wait of step A. Tracker is plan v4 M5. Loop is M6 with retirement step 3.8.
- "Load those artifacts again and use them": steps A5 and C3 use the new artifacts in this session (live reload is verified).
- Fable as advisor or orchestrator: step A2 writes both roles with their conditions and cost. This session is the orchestrator case: it already spans more than one context window.
- Model table from models.dev: step B.
- Owner goal points: 1 steps A1 and C2; 4 and 5 step A; 6 step C; 12 steps A5, B and C. Points 2 and 3 are measured (7.2 s), not changed. Points 9 and 10 are held by the `docs-claims` and `no-comments` hooks on every commit.

## Alternatives rejected

| Alternative | Evidence | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M2b as written | 7.2 s Markdown commit against a 10 s target; no measured gain from moving hooks to CI | owner decision 2 |
| Regenerate the model map and edit 35 files today | the Claude hook writes aliases, and the aliases already reach the 5.5 and 5.2 models; 25 test files pin old ids | decided on the step B table; owner decision 3 |
| Rerun the pilot with 5 attempts per arm | the expected gain is 20 to 30 k tokens and the spread between trials is 150 k; the pilot runs on Codex | one repetition, counts only |
| Always-on rewrite under 600 words | does not fit; needs the full inventory | stays at M8; step C is its first measured cut |
| Advisor key and an `env` projection in the settings code | `/advisor fable` exists; `.claude/settings.json` has no `env` block and no code writes one | filed as a record |
| Engine tier for integrity level L3 (`src/basicly/integrity.py:95` selects `maximum`) | belongs to the loop, which is retired at M6 | filed as a record, named in the roles rule as a known exception |
| Engine reduction, backlog labels | no measured user gain in one session | plan v4 order |

## Working shape

Fable 5.2 plans, writes briefs, reviews diffs and accepts. It edits catalog text itself. One Opus worker at a time writes code (step A4). Step B is read-only and runs first. Reviewers are fresh Sonnet agents; the Haiku `tester` runs suites. There is one writer in the checkout at any time. Catalog sources under `.basicly/core/` and `.basicly-local/` are edited, never the generated files; after an edit, `uv run basicly build`, `uv run basicly skills-build` and `uv run basicly agents-build` regenerate them before any done command runs.

## Step 0: record and baseline (15 minutes)

- 0.1 File one feature record under basicly-gtb19bg with children A, B and C, each with its done commands; put this plan on the feature record; claim them. Done: `python3 .basicly/core/kit/tracker/cli.py show .basicly/ledger FEATURE-ID` prints the plan text and lists 3 children.
- 0.2 Owner action, optional: `git config basicly.holder NAME` before the first claim (finding basicly-d6cfl4v).
- 0.3 Comment the measured commit time and output size on basicly-gtb19bg.40.
- Every step is one commit, staged by explicit path, and that commit is its revert unit. After each step, a comment on its child gives the commit id and the next command, so a new session can resume. If a worker fails or leaves uncommitted work, its files are restored from the last commit only after the owner confirms, and the step is redone from its brief.
- Pushes: one after step A and one after step C. A green CI run on main takes 23.5 minutes (measured on the last run). Step C runs during the first wait. A red run is fixed before any later push.

## Step A: model roles (90 minutes)

- A1 (5 min) Copy the verified vendor facts from `facts.md` to a closed research record: URL, quoted line and date for the cost table, the advisor rules, the delegation criterion and the alias table. Done: `show ID` prints the line "cost about a third less".
- A2 (20 min, after step B's table exists, so the tier table in the guidance uses it) The roles rule in one home: the body of the `tier-injection` skill, section "When the repository requires tier-only dispatch", which the tier kit ships as `GUIDANCE.md` (a test already requires the two to be equal). It states: who owns (Opus 5.5); the tier of delegated work (`medium` by default, `high` for a judgement, `low` only to run a suite); when to ask the Fable advisor (a problem that survived two failed approaches, or a decision that is hard to undo) and its measured cost; when Fable orchestrates (work larger than one context window, or routine work with a long cost tail) and its measured cost; raise effort before adding a model; the L3 exception. The kit's `INSTRUCTION.md` and the tier table in `GUIDANCE.md` are aligned with it. The skill description gains the triggers "delegate", "which model", "advisor". This repository's local always-on line "Model Tier Routing" names the two Fable roles and points to the skill, in at most 40 words; consumers get no new always-on text. Done: `uv run basicly check` and `uv run basicly skills-check` exit 0; `uv run pytest tests/test_kit_packages.py -q` passes; `rg -c 'advisor' .claude/skills/tier-injection/SKILL.md` and `rg -c 'orchestrat' .claude/skills/tier-injection/SKILL.md` each print a count above 0.
- A3 (15 min) Tiers in the review skills. Five of the 12 lens rows name a defined agent, which carries its own tier; the 7 `general-purpose` rows take the default that A4 gives. So the Launch step of swarm gains one line: an agent takes its definition's tier, a `general-purpose` agent takes the repository default, and a lens that needs more names `high`, passed as the `alias` field of the JSON that `python3 .basicly/core/kit/tier/tier_resolver.py --host claude --tier high` prints. The council brief says to keep `findings` empty and shows the three allowed severities, which closes the defect that voided 5 votes today. `architect` moves to `tier: high`. One catalog test, which imports the tier list from `src/basicly/schema.py`, fails for a catalog agent on `maximum`, and its message names the remedy (`tier: high`). Done: `uv run pytest tests/test_swarm_check.py tests/test_swarm_council.py tests/test_swarm_climb.py tests/test_skill_standard.py -q` passes, plus every test file that `rg -l 'swarm|council|hill-climb|tier-injection|architect' tests` lists; `rg -l '^tier: maximum' .claude/agents` prints nothing, and the control `rg -l '^tier: high' .claude/agents` prints 8 files (7 before).
- A4 (30 min, one Opus worker) Spawn-time default, hook only. `claude_tier_hook.py` passes the resolver's existing default-tier input (the environment variable `tier_resolver.py` already reads; the worker confirms its name from the code) for a start that names `general-purpose` or no agent type, and no `model`. An explicit `model`, any other agent type and a set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` are left alone. An invalid value, and the value `maximum`, print one warning with the valid list, and the start proceeds unchanged; the worker first checks in the live hook documentation where a PreToolUse hook's warning becomes visible, and uses that channel. One parametrized test with eight named cases: default applied; explicit model kept; variable unset; invalid value; omitted agent type; override variable set; other agent type; an exception inside the resolver, which must give exit 0, no output and an unchanged start, so a faulty hook can never block an agent start. This repository sets the variable to `medium` by hand in the `env` block of `.claude/settings.local.json`, which git ignores on this machine; other repositories get the default only when they set the variable, and the roles rule says so. Undo order if agent starts misbehave: remove the variable from `.claude/settings.local.json` first, then revert the A4 commit. Done: `printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Agent","tool_input":{"subagent_type":"general-purpose","prompt":"x"}}' | BASICLY_DEFAULT_TIER=medium python3 .basicly/core/kit/tier/claude_tier_hook.py | jq -r .hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput.model` prints `sonnet` (variable name as confirmed); the same input with `"model":"opus"` prints nothing; `jq -r .env.BASICLY_DEFAULT_TIER .claude/settings.local.json` prints `medium`; the tier kit test files pass; the commit passes the `no-comments` hook.
- A5 (15 min) First use, second use and measurement. The diff of A2 to A4 is reviewed through the new skill text with two lenses: the agents take their tier from the definition or the default. Record tokens and duration from the task usage, the findings, and how many a fresh verifier confirms, on a research record, with the limit named: one run per cell is an observation. One of the reviewers is a `general-purpose` agent started with no model: its reported model must be a Sonnet model, which proves the hook default in the live session. If it is not, the comment on child A says the session did not reload the hook or the `env` block, and the probe moves to the next session. Findings are fixed before the push.
- Commit the tracker comments in one `chore(tracker)` commit, push, and let CI run during step C.

## Step B: model table (15 minutes, one read-only agent, first, while step 0 and A1 run)

Fetch `https://models.dev/api.json` once into the scratchpad. For each vendor in `.basicly/core/models/anchors.yaml`, list the newest model per tier on each surface the map names, and mark each anchor current or stale. Done: the table is a comment on child B and is shown to the owner with one recommendation per stale anchor. The owner decides on regeneration from the table; it is not part of this session's budget. If it is chosen, it is one more step of about 45 minutes after step C: `anchors.yaml`, `.scripts/generate_model_map.py`, the tests that read the generated map, reverted if more than 8 test files fail.

## Step C: instruction trim and quiet hook output (80 minutes, during the first CI run)

- C1 (10 min) Counts before. Probe: `codex --version` prints a version (0.167.0 today). One pilot run on the unchanged tree: `uv run python .scripts/eval_harness_trials.py --family codex --model gpt-5.6-sol --effort medium --arm plain=FILE --arm gates-only=FILE --arm full-basicly=FILE --cases CASES.JSON --repetitions 1 --timeout 180 --output A-FOLDER-IN-THE-SCRATCHPAD`, with the recorded arm and case files under `.basicly/usage/harness-redesign/value-pilot/` (the evaluator accepts only these three arms together; about 2 minutes). From the full-basicly transcript, record: skill files read, model calls, instruction tokens injected per call. For each skill file read, name the text that caused it: an instruction line or a skill description in the listing. Record `wc -w AGENTS.md` in a scratch consumer install. If Codex or the model is unavailable, the counts are reported as not run, and C2, C3 and C5 still ship.
- C2 (30 min) Inventory first, on record basicly-gtb19bg.30.3: one row per line of the fragments under `.basicly/core/fragments/` that the cut would change, with its verdict (keep; enforced by a named gate; moved to a named skill; dropped) and its new home. Then the cut, in those fragments only, because the pilot arm and every consumer load them. The targets are the texts C1 named as causes. The lines of Harness Loop, Quality Gate and Session Completion already carry triggers ("At session end", "when useful", "For a failed check") and were in place when the pilot agent still read those skills, so a new trigger word is not a fix: the line is removed where the skill listing already says the same, or the skill description is narrowed so that a small task does not match it. Rules follow the Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 prompting pages: scope and reason in the rule, exceptions in the rule. No line under "Never do" or "Ask first" is cut.
- C3 (10 min) Gate before shipping, all three required: every test file that `rg -l 'CLAUDE.md|AGENTS.md|guidance' tests` lists passes, with a moved sentence's test pointing at its new home; `uv run basicly check` exits 0; one fresh Sonnet reviewer, started through the A3 skill text, checks every inventory row against the tree and reports each rule that lost its only home. Any such rule is restored.
- C4 (5 min) Counts after: rerun C1 on the trimmed tree. Done: a comment on child C with the three counts and the word count of the consumer `AGENTS.md`, before and after. The verdict is on the counts, never on total tokens: one run cannot show a token gain. A failed acceptance in the trimmed run means the trim is reverted.
- C5 (30 min) Quiet hook output. Facts: a passing one-file commit prints 10,220 bytes; the last session made 21 commits (`git log`), about 215 KB or 60 k tokens of hook text. `.basicly/lefthook.yml` is rendered by `src/basicly/lefthook_config.py`; `.basicly/bin/lefthook --help` names `LEFTHOOK_OUTPUT` and a config option `output`. Probe first, 5 minutes: one real commit of this session with `LEFTHOOK_OUTPUT=failure,summary` (value confirmed from the Lefthook 2.2.2 documentation through `interface-facts`), bytes counted. If the bytes fall, set the option in `lefthook_config.py`. If the followed dispatch command still prints everything, quiet the pass path in `.basicly/core/hooks/lefthook-runtime.py`: one summary line on a pass, everything on a failure. Tests: a failing hook prints the failed check and its remedy as today; a passing hook that prints a warning line keeps that line; a passing run prints less than 1,000 bytes. Done: the bytes of one real passing commit against 10,220; `uv run basicly hooks-check` exits 0. If neither path works in 30 minutes, C5 stops and a record holds the finding.
- Commit the tracker comments, push and wait for CI.

## Step D: release (owner decision 4, 35 minutes with its waits)

- Before the cut, test the path a consumer takes: install `--ref v0.43.0` into a scratch repository, add one hand edit to a managed file and one agent definition with `tier: maximum`, then install the new wheel over it and run `basicly check`, `basicly skills-check` and `basicly agents-check`. The output goes on the feature record. A failure means no cut.
- Changelog fragments for A and C. `uv run basicly release 0.44.0 --issue FEATURE-ID --dry-run`, then the real cut. Push main and the tag in one command, so the pinned install commands in the docs never point at a missing tag. Never while main is red.
- A cut that is wrong before the push is undone only with the owner's confirmation (delete the local tag, return to the commit before the cut). After the push, a bad release is fixed forward as 0.44.1; a tag is not withdrawn. A consumer can pin the previous release with `sh install.sh --ref v0.43.0`.
- Update the WSL and Windows installs. Done: `basicly --version` prints 0.44.0 on both.

## Step E: close (10 minutes)

File the deferred records: the map regeneration if not done; one-line hook output; a Claude arm for the value evaluator; the `env` projection; the L3 engine tier; the machine path in the pilot's `cases.json`. Write the session handover on basicly-gtb19bg. Correct the memory note that says agents and hooks need a restart.

## Budget and cut line

Step B 15 inside step 0 and A1; step 0 15; A 85; C 80, during the first CI run; second CI wait 25; D 35; E 10. About 4.2 hours of wall time. Cut lines: C5 is dropped first if step C runs long. Step C does not start after the 2.5 hour mark; its child stays open. Step D is skipped if step C ends after the 3.5 hour mark; the work stays on main, green, and the release is the first step of the next session.

## How this can fail

| Risk | Probe | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sonnet reviewers miss defects | A5 | raise the lens to `high` in the column |
| The hook default reaches a wrong agent | the eight named test cases | scope is `general-purpose` or no type; unset restores inherit |
| The running session does not reload the hook | A5 | say so; probe next session |
| models.dev lacks an id on a surface | step B table | no regeneration offered |
| A trimmed line was a rule's only home | inventory before the cut, C3 reviewer | restore the line |
| A hook fault blocks agent starts | the eighth test case | remove the variable, then revert A4 |
| Quiet output hides a warning that passed | C5 test on a failing hook; the runner's own summary line stays | restore the Lefthook setting |
| One pilot run misleads | counts only, no token verdict | report the counts as an observation |
| Codex unavailable | C1 probe | C4 not run, said plainly |
| CI red after a push | 23.5 minute wait after each push | fix first; no release on red |
| The release breaks a consumer | scratch consumer install and downgrade before the cut | no cut; fix forward |
| A worker fails or the session stops | a comment with commit id and next command after each step | resume from the feature record |

## Decisions for the owner

1. Approve the plan (`go`). This covers edits to skills, agents, fragments, the tier kit, `.claude/settings.local.json`, and one network read of models.dev.
2. Approve the deviation from plan v4: M2b "7 hooks, others to CI" is not done now, because a commit takes 7.2 s. Recommended: yes.
3. Decided by the owner on 2026-11-10: probe models.dev today, decide on regeneration from the table.
4. Release v0.44.0 at the end if the cut line allows (recommended).
5. Set your saved default model to Opus 5.5 and name Fable through `/advisor fable` or an explicit session choice (recommended: Anthropic measured Fable alone at 1.5 to 2.4 times the cost of Opus 5.5 for 1.6 to 5.9 points). It costs no session time and acts on every later session.
6. Optional: a holder name for step 0.2.

payload.title: Print one summary line for a passing commit inside the basicly check runner

payload.text: [finding 2026-11-10] The Lefthook output setting was tried and stopped. Probe on real commits with LEFTHOOK_OUTPUT=summary,failure: a passing commit printed 522 bytes in place of about 9500, and a failing commit-msg hook still printed its whole reason (1294 bytes). A worker then set it as the default for git hooks in lefthook-runtime.py and measured a passing pre-commit at 71 bytes in place of 3614. It was not shipped, because the setting hides every line a passing hook prints, and some of those lines are notices a person needs: the post-merge advice to run tracker fold (two cases of tests/test_native_tracker_fold_advice.py failed), the check runner's auto-fix failures and its auto-fixed and re-staged line, the pre-push scope and fallback notices, and informational lines of tracker-claim, identity-guard and markdownlint. Lefthook cannot separate a notice from routine output. ## Result of the M5 storage hill-climb, 2026-11-10

Survey: three Opus researchers, 17 solution families (comment on basicly-gtb19bg.43). Climb: 5 rounds, 5 fresh reviewers per round (Sonnet lenses, Opus alternatives lens), 4 Sonnet verifiers, stopped at the cap of 5 rounds. Score per property is the lowest reviewer grade; cells show low-high.

| property | r1 | r2 | r3 | r4 | r5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| n1-no-pr-conflict | 6-9 | 6-9 | 6-9 | 7-9 | 7-9 |
| n2-local-writers | 6 | 6-8 | 6-8 | 7-8 | 7-8 |
| n3-code-sync | 4-7 | 4-6 | 4-7 | 4-7 | 5-8 |
| n4-shared-in-time | 3-6 | 5-7 | 5-7 | 5-7 | 6-8 |
| c2-file-count | 9-10 | 9-10 | 9-10 | 9-10 | 9-10 |
| c3-visible | 6-9 | 5-9 | 7-9 | 5-9 | 7-9 |
| operability | 3-5 | 4-6 | 3-6 | 5-6 | 5-6 |
| important findings | 25 | 23 | 24 | 25 | 30 |

decision: stop: the cap of 5 rounds is reached

Contraction: a separate backlog repository with one linear event log (one file per writer), claims decided by first claim in log order, close derived from closes/refs/none declarations on the code default branch. Claim branches with an empty-lease push (v3) were dropped in v4 as a second source of truth. Verified by fresh agents on local bare repositories: empty-lease create refuses an existing branch; claim re-check after a refused push makes log claims exclusive; a plain bypassing push lands a duplicate claim, hence the fold rule; git revert keeps the subject inside Revert "...".

## Round 5 findings, open (not yet verified by a fresh agent)

- alternatives (Opus): the orphan `tracker` branch in the code repository may meet every property as well and is simpler: no second repository, no attach, no manifest, no cross-repository CI secret. Its argument rests on the climb rubric, which allowed "ordinary visible branches"; the owner's C3 text says "git refs and git notes are out", and a branch is a ref. This is owner decision 1.
- alternatives: the code repository's scheduled `fsck --code` reads a private backlog, so every consumer needs a cross-repository read token, which v5 does not name.
- alternatives: a share that rebases while another process appends can fail or lose the append, because LedgerLock covers only append and commit. Fix: keep queued events uncommitted and build one commit on the fetched head under the lock, or hold LedgerLock across fetch, rebase and ref update.
- alternatives and simplicity: v5 has grown past the never-events. Smaller first release: per-writer log, share with the first-claim fold rule, closes/refs/none with revert handling, fsck --code, migrate --to-backlog. Later: writers.toml identity, signing, non-fast-forward fetch check, CODEOWNERS, BACKLOG.md workflow, --restore, takeover, 7-day expiry, the backlog pre-push hook.
- feasibility: a rebase merge drops the PR title, so the declaration is lost; require it in the head commit or forbid rebase merge. Close derivation needs a new code_history module (derivation.py derives phases, not git history) that reads the code repository. The 30 s claim deadline conflicts with an unstated share-lock timeout and 5 push rounds. Existing seam for the clone: git_layout.py:109-115. Estimate about 6 new and about 8 changed modules; build order: clone+share+fold rule, attach/detach/migrate, BACKLOG.md, declarations+hook, code history+fsck --code+CI, sandbox forge tests.
- recovery: idempotent retry after a share that pushed but did not record; an adopt event for a void claim already worked on; offline closes recorded as unverified; reverting the cutover PR; restore from a stale clone needs accept-head; BACKLOG.md workflow needs a concurrency group.
- poka-yoke: takeover should require a prior logged release; the PR check should resolve the id and holder; a push-triggered fsck workflow in the backlog; refuse hand edits to BACKLOG.md and hand-made clones; minimum tool version in manifest.toml and tracker.toml; one shared declaration parser.
- Conflicts between lenses to resolve in design: simplicity says BACKLOG.md optional, ux (round 4) says required for C3; simplicity says drop the share re-check, ux and alternatives (round 4) need a definite claim result.

## Final graded note (version 5)

# M5 contraction note, version 5: where the conflict-free tracker stores its data

Status: concept level. This note picks one storage approach. It is not a design; no code exists.

## The requirement (owner, record basicly-gtb19bg.43)

Never-events:

- N1: two pull requests (PRs) are open, both edit the same tracker file, one merges, the other gets a merge conflict.
- N2: several agents on one machine and one repository write the same tracker file, overwrite each other, corrupt it or need resolution work.
- N3: the tracker is out of sync with the actual code.
- N4: tracker state is not shared with the other developers in time.

Constraints:

- C2: not thousands of tracker files in the code repository; a backlog can pass 10000 stories.
- C3: nothing hidden. A person sees the data in ordinary tools (GitHub and Bitbucket web UI) and can find and remove it without inside knowledge. Git refs other than ordinary branches, and git notes, are out.

## Facts (checked 2026-11-10)

Confirmed:

- GitHub ignores user-defined `.gitattributes` merge drivers for PR mergeability (community discussion 9288). Only disjoint paths prevent N1.
- Bitbucket Cloud issue tracker endpoints were removed on 2026-08-20 (Atlassian community post 3193882).
- A plain non-force push is refused when the branch moved since the pusher's last fetch (gitprotocol-pack).
- Verified twice with local bare repositories (two and three clones): claims written as log events on one linear branch are exclusive when the claimer re-checks after every refused push; without the re-check every claim lands. A writer who bypasses the tool with plain `git pull --rebase && git push` also lands a duplicate claim, because per-writer files never conflict.
- `git revert` keeps the reverted subject inside `Revert "..."` and writes "This reverts commit <sha>" in the body; a merge revert adds "reversing changes made to <sha>".
- The default `GITHUB_TOKEN` is limited to the repository that runs the workflow (docs.github.com).
- GitHub's default squash message for a one-commit PR is the commit's title; the REST API exposes the setting as `squash_merge_commit_title`, so a CI check can read it.
- Blocking force-push and deletion on GitHub: "in public repositories owned by a GitHub Free organization" and "in all repositories owned by an organization using GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise Cloud" (about-protected-branches). A private backlog on a free plan cannot block them.
- 269 of the last 300 commit subjects here end with a record id (`git log -300 --format=%s | grep -cE '(basicly|dev)-[a-z0-9.]+\)?$'`), while basicly-gtb19bg and basicly-gtb19bg.12, the two most named, are in progress: naming a record is not closing it.
- Today's kit: the writer name is a slug of the branch (`events.py:779-792`); the lock file name is at `events.py:65` and `LedgerLock` at `events.py:901`, with a 5 s timeout that raises (`events.py:97`, `:942`); the event actor and holder are client-set (`events.py:253`, `:263`; `holders.py:34-38`); claims are read from log events (`claims.py:99`); the commit hook interpolates the ledger path into double-quoted shell text and skips silently without the ledger (`claim_block.py:50-70`, basicly-7b2t44m).

Prior art: git-issue (a separate issues repository), TrackDown (status from commit messages), actions-mutex (a refused branch push as a lock), an agent pattern in which "git rejects the second push" of a task claim (agentpatterns.ai), and beads (an agent tracker whose format this kit reads: first a JSONL file in the code repository, now Dolt data under `refs/dolt/data`, which fails C3). Nothing found combines a visible backlog repository, a linear event log with re-checked claims and a code-derived close; that combination is the only new part.

Open, to settle on sandbox repositories before design: Bitbucket's squash message default and its branch rules per plan.

## Recommended: a separate backlog repository with one linear log

### Where the data lives

- A repository `<code-repo>-backlog` on the same forge. Its default branch holds one append-only event file per writer, `writers.toml` (one line per writer: id, display name, forge login), `manifest.toml` (the code repository URL) and `BACKLOG.md`.
- `BACKLOG.md` is required: a readable table of records, status, holder and linked commits, with a "generated at" time. A scheduled workflow in the backlog repository writes it through the same share step as any writer; a failed run shows as a failed workflow. Writers never edit it.
- The code repository holds one tracked file, `.basicly/tracker.toml`, with the backlog URL, plus one README line.

### Writers on one machine (N2)

- One backlog clone per machine, in the user state folder under a name hashed from the backlog URL, mode 0700, outside every code checkout and worktree.
- Writer id: random, created once per clone, stored inside the clone's `.git` folder with a hash of the machine id; a copied clone makes a new id. Never derived from the branch name.
- `LedgerLock` covers only the local append and commit. The share lock covers the push.
- Each event carries the writer id and a session id.
- A pre-push hook inside the clone refuses any push not started by the tool, and names `basicly tracker share`.

### The one ordering rule (N4)

- The fold reads the default branch in commit order. The first open claim of a record wins; a later claim on a held record is void and reported. This rule, in one place, decides claims, so a bypassing writer can never take a claim.
- Share: push; if refused, fetch, rebase (own file only), re-check every claim in the batch against the fold, drop and report a claim another writer holds, push again; up to 5 rounds with random back-off. The re-check exists for fast feedback; the fold rule is the guarantee.
- A claim waits on the share lock and its share, with a 30 s deadline. It ends in one of: "claimed", "held by <name> since <time>", or "not claimed: the forge did not answer in 30 s; run claim again". A claim that did not land is never queued and never held.
- Non-exclusive events (comments, fields) queue when the forge is unreachable. Every command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share". A pre-push hook in each code checkout prints the same line, so a developer sees it before going home.
- Claims are refreshed by every share of their holder. A claim with no refresh for 7 days can be released by any writer with a logged reason. Each command shows the holder's own claims with their expiry.

### Closing (N3)

- One authority closes a record that has code: the code default branch. A record that never had a linked commit (research, decisions) closes by a backlog `close` event. `fsck` reports a backlog close on a record with linked commits.
- Declarations: `closes <id>`, `refs <id>`, `none`. The PR title must carry one; a bare id is refused. Commits inside a PR need none. A direct push to the default branch must carry one in every commit.
- Derivation over the first-parent history of the code default branch: revert commits are classified first by their "This reverts commit <sha>" body; a revert undoes exactly the declaration of the commit it names, and a merge revert undoes the declarations of the merged range. The latest effect wins, so a revert of a revert closes again.
- The local commit hook fetches the backlog clone first, then refuses an unknown id or a `closes` by a non-holder; `closes <id> takeover` overrides and is reported by `fsck`. `closes` is refused when the last successful fetch is older than one day.
- The PR check reads the title from an environment variable on `pull_request` (never `pull_request_target`), refuses a missing declaration, and checks `squash_merge_commit_title` through the API on GitHub. On Bitbucket it requires the declaration in every commit until the squash default is known.
- A scheduled CI job in the code repository runs the existing `fsck` in a `--code` mode and lists commits with no declaration, takeovers and claims on closed records, each with its repair command.

### Trust and tamper detection

- Every writer can push to the backlog, as every developer can push to the code repository. The tool, not the forge, enforces the rules; detection covers what the forge does not prevent.
- `fsck` compares each event's writer id with `writers.toml` and with the commit author, and reports a mismatch. Commit signing (verified on the forge) is the recommended hardening; without it, identity is as strong as the code repository's own commit authorship.
- Every clone keeps the last fetched head and refuses a fetch that is not a fast-forward, so a history rewrite is detected by the first clone that fetches. Blocking force-push and deletion on the forge is required where the plan allows it (public repositories, or GitHub Team and Enterprise for private ones); `attach` warns when it is not set.
- `fsck` reports a changed line in any existing event, a deleted event and a void claim. The backlog workflow and `fsck` sit under a CODEOWNERS rule where the forge supports it.
- `attach` shows the typed URL and asks for confirmation the first time; only `https` and `ssh` URLs; a URL with credentials is refused. `manifest.toml` is checked, not trusted.
- Event text is validated against the event schema, escaped in `BACKLOG.md`, and never passed to a shell or a workflow expression. Every hook path passes through an environment variable (basicly-7b2t44m, all six sites).
- Agents use a token scoped to the backlog repository. The kit recommends a private backlog.

### Commands a person meets

- `attach <url>` (first day; again after a rename, carrying the queue; `--restore <clone>` to rebuild a lost backlog), `share`, `detach`, and the existing `migrate` with a `--to-backlog` mode. `sync` keeps its current meaning.
- After `attach` writes `tracker.toml`, every in-repository ledger command refuses with "this repository uses a backlog: run basicly tracker attach", and the upgrade reinstalls the hooks.

### Recovery

- Every machine clone is a full copy. `attach --restore` runs `fsck` on the clone, requires an empty target repository and asks for confirmation of the head commit before it pushes.
- `detach` refuses while the clone holds commits the forge does not have, and names `share`.
- Migration: `migrate --to-backlog` imports the old ledger keyed by event id and resumes after a crash. Cutover: one code PR adds `tracker.toml` and deletes `.basicly/ledger`; afterwards a CI check refuses any PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` and names `migrate --to-backlog --branch`. Same id with different content is reported and the first kept. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records. The old ledger stays in code history.
- Removal: `detach` on each machine, delete `.basicly/tracker.toml` in a code PR, archive or delete the backlog repository.

### Reuse

- Reused: the event format and fold (`events.py`, `claims.py`, `derivation.py`), `fsck.py`, `migrate.py`, `LedgerLock`, `holders.py`, the hook builder (`claim_block.py`, `install_hook.py`).
- New: the machine clone and share step, `attach` and `detach`, the declaration check in hook and CI, the `--code` mode of `fsck`, the `BACKLOG.md` generator, the CI templates.
- A consumer without the basicly engine gets all of it from the tracker kit, with the CI parts as templates.

## Rejected candidates

- Claim branches with an empty-lease push: a second source of truth for claims and an untested forge lease.
- One branch per writer: writer branches accumulate and the default branch no longer shows the data. Kept as the fallback for comments and fields if the contention test below fails.
- An orphan `tracker` branch in the code repository: every clone fetches it; C2 and C3 need an owner ruling.
- Today's design repaired: a claim on a branch is visible only after merge, so N4 fails by structure.

## Proof tests

- In CI on local bare repositories: N2, N3, N4, contention and migration. At each release on sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories: N1, the forge settings and the squash defaults.
- N1: 1000 tracker writes from a code checkout leave `git status --porcelain` empty; two code PRs that both ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees write 1000 events against a forge stub with 1 s push latency; every event lands once; no command waits more than 1 s for `LedgerLock`; a copied clone gets a new writer id.
- N3: two `refs` PRs keep a record open; a `closes` PR closes it; its revert reopens it; the revert of the revert closes it; a merge revert reopens the records its range closed; squash, merge and rebase merges keep the declaration; a bare id and a non-holder `closes` are refused; a direct push without a declaration is listed by `fsck --code`.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones claim one record at once and exactly one wins; a bypassing plain push of a second claim is void in the fold and reported; an offline claim is refused; a claim past its 30 s deadline reports "not claimed" and is not held later.
- Contention: 6 clones with 1 s push latency and continuous writes; 99 percent of claims end within 10 s and none ends unclear. If this fails, comments and fields move to one branch per writer and only claims, releases and closes stay on the default branch.
- Migration: `migrate --to-backlog` killed at each step resumes to equal records.

payload.text: [correction 2026-11-10] The C3 line in the note (from version 2 on) and the c3 line of the climb rubric say git refs other than ordinary branches are out. That is the climb's reading, not the owner's. The owner's text on basicly-gtb19bg.43 (comment seqs 9 and 10) says tracker data must not live in git refs or git notes, with no exception for branches. The round 5 argument that an orphan tracker branch is as good and simpler was scored against the looser reading. Round 5 Verify did not run: its findings are unverified, although the climb state records --refuted 0. The climb stopped at the cap, not by convergence; important findings went from 25 to 30.

[verify 2026-11-11, Opus, kit fit] L1 confirmed: derivation.py derives phase from folded status only (derive_phase :129-152); the kit runs no git subprocess (only holders.py:71 reads git config; install_hook.py:68 is hook shell text), so code-history derivation is a new module with its own git runner; git_layout.git_dir and hooks_dir can be reused. L2 partly refuted: the redirect (git_layout.py:115-118, :70-94) needs a .basicly/ledger directory in the checkout holding an absolute-path redirect file and a matching path inside the target; it disappears at cutover, so it is not the seam. Places that assume an in-repo ledger: claim_block.py:57 and :63-72, install_hook.py:44-52 and :84-85, locate.py:70 and :82, cli.py:254-282 (commit-check), commands.py:70-74. L3 confirmed: GITHUB_TOKEN is limited to its own repository (docs.github.com GITHUB_TOKEN page); derivation is local on every machine and needs no credential; only a scheduled audit needs one (a read-only deploy key or app token, or the audit in the backlog CI for a public code repository); a pre-push check alone misses forge-side merges. L4 confirmed: the fold orders by (record, seq, id) (events.py:270-272), dedupes by event id (:287-295), marks a record forked on equal seq (:693-696); two concurrent claims at one seq are won by the larger content hash, not by push order (probe run). First-claim-in-log-order needs a git-aware read layer that orders events by first-parent commit order of the backlog default branch before the fold; client timestamps (events.py:263) cannot serve.

[verify 2026-11-11, Opus, git mechanics, local bare repositories] K1 confirmed: a rebase-based share loses appends (stress run: 6 of 6 rebases failed, 170 of 194 appends landed on a detached HEAD, none reached the remote; an aborted rebase dropped an append). Safe and tested: events wait in a queue file inside .git; LedgerLock covers only queue read and remove-by-id; the commit is built with a temporary index and commit-tree on FETCH_HEAD and pushed outside the lock; 3 runs of 300 appends against a concurrent pusher gave 300 ids, 0 missing, 0 duplicates. Clearing the queue by byte offset loses appends. K2: a crash after push and before queue clear re-sends lines; the fold dedupes by content-derived event id (events.py:288-293, :686-688, :298); share must also filter queued ids already on the fetched head. K3: with 8 agents and 1 s latency claims took p50 4.1 s, max 4.1 s (40 of 40); with a nonstop remote pusher at 2 s latency p50 26 s, max 34 s, 10 unclear results; at 3 s none claimed. A promise that a failed claim is never held cannot be kept with batched shares: the claim answer must allow pending, resolved at the next fetch, and the deadline must cut off running git work. K4: GitHub rebase merge adds commits individually with no PR title (docs about-merge-methods); Bitbucket documents no default squash message.

## Context

The owner asked on 2026-11-10 for model routing decided by judgement and data, with the guideline that Opus 5.5 is the best daily balance and Fable 5.2 suits advice, orchestration and heavy thinking. An Opus swarm (evidence, cost, enforcement, devil's advocate) reviewed a draft; the vendor numbers were checked against the raw page by curl.

## Decision

| Work | Model | Effort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner session, coding, repair | Opus 5.5 | medium; high for hard bugs; never low for judgement work |
| Research, prior-art checks | Opus 5.5 | high |
| Review lenses, verifiers, council voters | Opus 5.5 | medium (provisional, unmeasured) |
| Stuck or hard-to-undo decision | Fable 5.2 advisor | default |
| Dedicated heavy-analysis or design session | Fable 5.2 as session owner | high |
| Fan-out parts of work larger than one context window | Sonnet 5.5 subagents under an Opus owner | high |
| Bulk work a test or gate checks | Sonnet 5.5 | high |
| Test runs, mechanical search | Haiku 5.5 | medium |
| Commit message | the owner session; Haiku only inside an agent that already commits | high |

Fable stays out of delegated worker and judge roles: no measurement supports it, and hill-climb, council and swarm leave the decision to a script or a proven merge.

## Evidence

Vendor page optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence (raw, 2026-11-10): DeepResearch Bench II, Opus 5.5 2.4 points above Sonnet 5.5 for 1.5 times the cost, Fable 5.2 2.9 times Opus for 1.9 points lower; defect search, Fable 5.2 alone at high F1 0.909, Opus 5.5 high 0.850, Opus with Sonnet subagents 0.831 for about a third less, Opus at low 0.489; Fable 5.2 orchestrator 19% more for the same score; Opus at low with a Fable advisor 7 points lower on Chartography. Local ledger: no per-model outcome data (dispatch events claude-opus-5 42, claude-sonnet-5 4, none for 5.5 or Fable).

## Work owed

- Agent definitions in the catalog that pin the routing: a review-lens and verifier agent at tier high, a project Explore agent at tier low; the swarm, hill-climb and council skills start them by name instead of naming the medium alias (swarm skill.yaml:21, lenses.md).
- The tier hook warns on or refuses a maximum-tier worker (basicly-gtb19bg.54); the model map moves to Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (basicly-gtb19bg.48); auto mode stops refusing a rewritten start (basicly-gtb19bg.53).
- tier-injection skill text and references/roles.md: add the scope of the Sonnet one-third figure (larger than one context window only), the research row, the Chartography loss and the Opus-at-low result.
- Log model plus verified and refuted findings per lens in each climb and swarm; run the paired experiment (one past climb round on Sonnet and on Opus, blind, scored by findings that survive verification) to settle the provisional row.

## Trigger
When the approved harness redesign reaches this slice, I want to load task context progressively and preserve required facts, so I can the current compact envelope can still append the full contract; reducing a wrapper size alone does not reduce delivered context.

## Proposed work
Replace redundant eager role/skill injection and unconditional historical hydration with task-relevant loading. Preserve critical acceptance criteria, constraints, source references and uncertainty immediately. Retrieve optional comments/artifacts by stable references with freshness checks. Bound tool output and preserve full evidence outside model context. Distinguish source code scope tokens, prompt tokens and repeated cached input.

## Reason
The current compact envelope can still append the full contract; reducing a wrapper size alone does not reduce delivered context.

## Related existing work

# M5 design, version 1: the conflict-free tracker, core release

Record: basicly-gtb19bg.43. Study: basicly-gtb19bg.58. Status: design for owner approval; no code exists.

## 1. Requirement and decisions

Never-events (owner, basicly-gtb19bg.43):

- N1: two open pull requests (PRs) edit the same tracker file; after one merges, the other cannot merge.
- N2: several agents on one machine write the same tracker file, overwrite each other, corrupt it or need resolution work.
- N3: the tracker is out of sync with the code.
- N4: tracker state is not shared with the other developers in time.

Constraints: C2, no thousands of tracker files in the code repository. C3, nothing hidden: the data is visible in the forge web UI and can be found and removed without inside knowledge; git refs and git notes are out.

Owner decisions of 2026-11-11: no tracker branch in the code repository; core first, hardening deferred; a readable `BACKLOG.md` is optional.

## 2. Where the data lives

Backlog repository, `<code-repo>-backlog`, on the same forge as the code:

- `log/<writer-id>.jsonl`: one append-only event file per writer. The number of files follows the number of writer clones, not records or events.
- `manifest.toml`: the URL of the one code repository this backlog belongs to, and the tracker format version.
- Nothing else is required. `BACKLOG.md` is optional (section 10).

Code repository:

- `.basicly/tracker.toml`: the backlog URL. This is the only tracker file in the code repository (C2).
- One README line names the backlog repository (C3: found without inside knowledge).

## 3. The machine clone

- One clone of the backlog repository per machine, in the user state folder, in a folder named by a hash of the backlog URL, mode 0700. All worktrees and all agents on the machine share it. It lives outside every code checkout, so `git clean` in a checkout cannot touch it.
- Writer id: random, made once per clone, stored inside the clone's `.git` folder together with a hash of the machine id. If the machine id differs at start (a copied clone), the tool makes a new writer id before it writes. The branch name is never used: a branch-derived name makes two machines share one file (`events.py:776-791`).
- Queue: `.git/basicly-queue.jsonl` inside the clone. It is outside the working tree, so git never commits it by itself.

## 4. Writing (N2)

- Every tracker write appends one event to the queue under `LedgerLock` (`events.py:901`). The lock covers only this append, which takes milliseconds.
- Each event carries a unique event id, the writer id and a session id. Two agents on one machine are told apart by the session id.

## 5. Sharing (N4)

`share` runs under a separate share lock. A command that does not need the result (a comment, a field) tries the share lock without waiting and returns; the holder of the lock shares everything in the queue.

One share attempt:

1. `git fetch` the default branch.
2. Under `LedgerLock`: read the queue. Release the lock.
3. Drop every queued event whose id is already on the fetched head (a crash after an earlier push re-sends nothing).
4. Build the commit with git plumbing, outside the lock: a temporary index from the fetched head, the writer's own file with the queued events appended, `commit-tree` with the fetched head as parent. The working tree and the local branch are never moved, so no rebase and no checkout exist.
5. `git push <commit>:<default branch>` (plain, never forced). The server refuses it if the branch moved.
6. On success, under `LedgerLock`, remove the shared events from the queue by event id, never by position: an append made during the push stays. On refusal, go to step 1. Stop after 5 attempts with random back-off; the events stay queued and every command reports "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share".

Verified 2026-11-11 on local bare repositories: a rebase-based share lost appends (170 of 194 on a detached HEAD in a stress run); this plumbing share kept 300 of 300 appends with no duplicates against a concurrent pusher, three runs. The fold also drops duplicate event ids (`events.py:288-293`), and ids derive from content (`events.py:298`).

## 6. Reading and the claim rule

- The read layer reads the default branch of the machine clone in first-parent commit order and, inside each commit, in the order of the lines it added. This order is the same on every machine.
- It drops duplicate event ids, then hands the events to the existing fold in that order.
- The claim rule: for each record, the first open claim in this order wins. A later claim on a held record is void and reported. The rule lives in the read layer, in one place, so a writer who bypasses the tool cannot take a claim.
- The current fold orders by `(record, seq, id)` and breaks a tie by content hash (`events.py:270-272`, `:693-696`). The read layer replaces that ordering for backlog ledgers; `seq` stays as a per-writer counter.

## 7. Claims

- A claim is an event. The claim command shares at once and waits for the result, with a 30 s deadline that kills any running git process. It reports one of three results, from the fold of the fetched head:
  - "claimed": the claim is on the default branch and is the first open claim.
  - "held by <name> since <time>": another claim came first; this one is void.
  - "pending: not yet on the forge; run basicly tracker claim --status <id> before you start work". A claim already in a push of another agent's batch may still land; the fold decides it at the next fetch, so a pending claim is never reported as failed.
- An agent starts work only on "claimed". The commit hook refuses a `closes` for a record the committer does not hold in the fold.
- Offline, a claim is refused with "claim needs the forge: run again when online".
- Measured 2026-11-11 with 8 agents on one machine: 1 s latency gave p50 4.1 s and max 4.1 s, all claimed; a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency gave p50 26 s with 10 pending results; at 3 s none landed in 30 s. Contention on one branch is the main risk of this design (section 15).
- Release is an event. A record that never had code closes by a backlog `close` event.

## 8. Closing a record from the code (N3)

- Declarations: every PR title, and every commit pushed straight to the code default branch, carries exactly one of `closes <id>`, `refs <id>` or `none`. A bare id is refused. One parser, used by the hook, the PR check and the derivation.
- Derivation: a new module reads the first-parent history of the code default branch through git. A commit with "This reverts commit <sha>" in its body undoes exactly the declaration of the commit it names; a merge revert undoes the declarations of the merged range. The latest effect wins. The kit runs no git process today (`derivation.py` derives phase only), so this module carries its own git runner and reuses `git_layout.git_dir`.
- Merge methods: squash merge with the PR title as the commit subject, or a merge commit (whose body carries the PR title). A rebase merge adds the commits one by one and carries no PR title (docs.github.com, about merge methods), so with rebase merge enabled every commit of the PR must carry a declaration. The PR check reads `squash_merge_commit_title` and `allow_rebase_merge` through the GitHub API and applies the stricter rule when either needs it. On Bitbucket, whose squash default is not documented, every commit carries a declaration.
- A record that has linked commits closes only from the code. A backlog `close` on such a record is reported by `fsck`.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: reads the machine clone, refuses a missing declaration, an unknown id or a bare id, and refuses when `tracker.toml` exists but no machine clone does, naming `basicly tracker attach <url>`. Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m).
- PR check in the code repository's CI: reads the PR title from an environment variable on the `pull_request` event, refuses a missing or bare declaration. It needs no access to the backlog.
- `fsck --code`: run by any developer or agent from its machine; needs no credential, because every machine holds both clones. It lists commits on code main with no declaration (admin merges, direct pushes), claims on closed records and backlog closes on records with code. A scheduled audit is optional: it needs a read-only deploy key for the backlog (deferred).

## 10. Optional readable view

- `basicly tracker board` and a CLI view already render records; they read the machine clone.
- A team that wants the backlog readable on the forge adds the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template to the backlog repository. It writes through the same share step as any writer.

## 11. Migration

- `basicly tracker migrate --to-backlog` imports the old ledger into the backlog keyed by event id, so it resumes after a crash. Acceptance (basicly-gtb19bg.43): a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
- Cutover: one code PR adds `.basicly/tracker.toml` and deletes `.basicly/ledger`. After it merges, the PR check refuses any PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` and names `migrate --to-backlog --branch` to move that branch's pending events.
- The old ledger stays in code history as the undo.

## 12. Kit changes

- New: the machine clone, queue and share step; the ordered read layer; the declarations parser; the code-history derivation; `attach` and `detach`; the PR check as a CI template; the `migrate --to-backlog` mode.
- Rewritten to read the machine clone: `claim_block.py` (hook), `cli.py` `commit-check`, `install_hook.py` (no in-repo ledger), `locate.py`, `commands.resolve_ledger`.
- Reused: event format, fold, `fsck.py`, `migrate.py`, `LedgerLock`, `holders.py`, `git_layout.git_dir`.
- A consumer with no basicly engine gets all of it from the tracker kit; the PR check ships as a CI template.

## 13. Proof tests

Run in CI on local bare repositories, except where named:

- N1: 1000 tracker writes from a code checkout leave `git status --porcelain` empty in the code repository. On sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories at each release: two code PRs that both ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees on one machine write 1000 events against a remote with 1 s push latency; every event lands exactly once; no command waits more than 1 s for `LedgerLock`; a process killed after its push and before its queue clear causes no duplicate in the fold; a copied clone gets a new writer id.
- N3: two `refs` PRs keep a record open; a `closes` PR closes it; its revert reopens it; the revert of that revert closes it; squash and merge-commit merges keep the declaration; a bare id is refused by the hook and the PR check; a direct push without a declaration is listed by `fsck --code`.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones claim one record at once and exactly one wins; a claim written by plain `git commit` and `git push`, bypassing the tool, is void in the fold; an offline claim is refused; a claim past its deadline reports "pending" and the next fetch resolves it to exactly one holder; with 8 agents and 1 s latency every claim resolves within 30 s.
- Migration: `migrate --to-backlog` killed at each step resumes to equal records.

## 14. Deferred (owner decision b)

Identity binding to forge accounts, commit signing, CODEOWNERS, the non-fast-forward fetch check, `attach --restore`, takeover, claim expiry, the backlog pre-push hook, the scheduled audit, the required `BACKLOG.md`.

## 15. Open facts

- Bitbucket Cloud's default squash message: not documented; the design requires a declaration per commit there.
- Contention on a real forge: measured only on local bare repositories with injected delay. A sandbox test at release measures claims per minute under many writers. If claims stay pending too long, comments and fields move to one branch per writer and only claims, releases and closes stay on the default branch.

# M5 design, version 2: the conflict-free tracker, core release

Record: basicly-gtb19bg.43. Study: basicly-gtb19bg.58. Design record: basicly-gtb19bg.60. Status: for owner approval; no code exists.

## 1. Requirement and decisions

Never-events (owner): N1, two open pull requests (PRs) edit the same tracker file and the second cannot merge; N2, agents on one machine overwrite each other, corrupt a file or need resolution work; N3, the tracker is out of sync with the code; N4, tracker state is not shared in time. Constraints: C2, no thousands of tracker files in the code repository; C3, nothing hidden (visible in the forge web UI, removable without inside knowledge; no git refs, no git notes).

Owner decisions of 2026-11-11: no tracker branch in the code repository; core first, hardening deferred; a readable `BACKLOG.md` is optional.

Kit rule that this design changes: the tracker kit's `SPEC.md:154` says the kit uses no network and no subprocess. The share step needs git and the network. This design adds one git module to the kit (section 12) and revises that line. This needs owner approval.

## 2. Where the data lives

Backlog repository, `<code-repo>-backlog`, on the same forge:

- `log/<writer-id>.jsonl`: one append-only event file per writer. A writer that bypasses the tool with `git pull --rebase` still cannot conflict, because no two writers touch one file (verified: the same bypass on one shared file conflicts).
- `manifest.toml`: the one code repository this backlog belongs to (its normalized URL) and the format version.

Code repository:

- `.basicly/tracker.toml`: the backlog URL. The only tracker file in the code repository (C2).
- One README line with the backlog URL. The PR check refuses a PR when `tracker.toml` exists and the README lacks the line, and prints the line to add (C3).

## 3. The machine clone

- One backlog clone per machine, in the user state folder, named by a hash of the backlog URL, mode 0700, outside every checkout. All worktrees and agents on the machine share it.
- Attaching needs read access; writing needs push rights. `attach` says which is missing and names the repository owner as the person to ask. A developer with read access only can commit code with `refs` declarations; claims and comments are refused by name.
- Writer id: random, made once per clone, stored in the clone's `.git` folder with a hash of the machine id; a copied clone makes a new writer id before it writes.
- `attach` compares the code repository's normalized origin URL with `manifest.toml` and refuses a mismatch: "this backlog belongs to <url>; attach its own backlog".
- Queue: `.git/basicly-queue.jsonl`. Under `LedgerLock`, before any read or append, a torn last line is cut back to the last newline. A line that does not parse is kept as it is, skipped and reported; it never blocks a share. The queue is rewritten only through a temporary file that replaces it.
- Last seen tip: the clone keeps the backlog head it last fetched.

## 4. Writing (N2)

- Every write appends one event to the queue under `LedgerLock`; the lock covers only the queue file.
- Each event has a content-derived event id (`events.py:298`), the writer id and a session id.
- After the append, the command tries a share without waiting (section 5), so an event leaves the machine as soon as the forge answers.

## 5. Sharing (N4)

One share attempt, with no separate share lock (two sharers that run at once both drop the events already on the fetched head):

1. `git fetch` the default branch.
2. If the last seen tip is not an ancestor of the fetched head (`merge-base --is-ancestor`), stop and refuse every share: "the backlog history was rewritten; events after <sha> are missing on the forge; run basicly tracker fsck". Verified: a force-pushed backlog lost every writer's history and the fetch exited 0.
3. Under `LedgerLock`, read the queue, then release the lock.
4. Drop every queued event whose id is already on the fetched head.
5. Build the commit with git plumbing, outside the lock: a temporary index from the fetched head, the writer's own file with the queued events appended, `commit-tree` with the fetched head as parent. The working tree and the local branch never move.
6. `git push <commit>:<default branch>`, plain, never forced. On success, record the new tip and, under `LedgerLock`, remove the shared events from the queue by event id.
7. On refusal, go to step 1. After 5 attempts with random back-off, the events stay queued; every command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share" once per command run, at the end of the output.

Verified on local bare repositories: this share kept 300 of 300 appends with no duplicates against concurrent pushers, three runs; a rebase-based share lost appends.

## 6. Reading and the claim rule

- The read layer reads the default branch in commit order (`git log --reverse --first-parent` with the lines each commit added), caches the result by head commit and extends it on the next fetch.
- It skips a line that does not parse, a line changed or deleted after it was added, and a line in a file whose header names another writer, and reports each in `fsck` with its commit and line.
- The fold gets an ordered mode: it keeps the input order, drops duplicate event ids and does not flag equal `seq` values as forked. `seq` and the running totals are computed by the fold from the order, not taken from the writer. The in-repo ledger keeps today's mode.
- The claim rule lives in the fold's holder logic (`_hold`, `events.py:602-614`): in the ordered mode, the first open claim of a record wins; a later claim on a held record is void and reported. One rule, one place.

## 7. Claims

- A claim is an event. `claim <id>` shares at once and waits, with a 30 s deadline that kills any running git process. Exit codes: 0 claimed; 3 held by another writer ("held by <name> since <time>; run basicly tracker claim <id> --take --reason <text> if the holder is gone"); 4 pending ("not yet on the forge; run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait").
- `--wait` blocks until the claim resolves or the deadline passes, so an agent never polls.
- A pending claim is never reported as failed: another agent's batch may still push it, and the fold decides it at the next fetch.
- An agent starts work only on exit code 0.
- A holder that is gone: the existing `claim --take` (`arguments.py:241`) records a takeover event with a reason; `fsck` lists takeovers. No expiry in the core.
- Offline, a claim is refused: "claim needs the forge: run again when online".
- Measured with 8 agents on one machine at 1 s latency: every claim within 4.1 s. With a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency the median was 26 s with 10 pending results; at 3 s none landed in 30 s. Contention is the main risk (section 15).

## 8. Closing a record from the code (N3)

- Declarations in commit messages. A record id at the end of the subject, as today, links the commit (`refs`); several ids are allowed. `closes <id>` closes a record. `reopens <id>` reopens one without reverting code. A PR or a direct push with no record carries `none`. One parser, built on the existing id parser (`claims.py:31`, `:53-58`).
- Derivation reads every commit reachable from the code default branch, in topological order, through the shared git module. A commit with "This reverts commit <sha>" undoes exactly the declarations of the commit it names; a merge revert undoes those of the merged range; the latest effect wins.
- Because it reads every reachable commit, a declaration survives squash, merge-commit and rebase merges as long as it is in a commit message on main. No forge API is read.
- A `closes` for an unknown record, or from a committer who does not hold the record in the fold, is void and reported by `fsck --code`; it never takes effect.
- A record that has linked commits closes only from the code. A record without code closes by a backlog `close` event.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: refuses a commit with no declaration, a bare `closes`, an unknown id, or a `closes` for a record the committer does not hold, after it fetches the clone. It refuses when `tracker.toml` exists and the clone is missing: "run basicly tracker attach <url>". Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m). The hook block carries a version marker.
- Every tracker command and the session start refuse when `tracker.toml` exists and the installed hook block lacks the current marker: "run basicly tracker install-hook".
- PR check in the code repository's CI (a template in the kit): refuses a PR in which no commit carries a declaration, a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` after cutover, and a missing README line. It reads the PR from the `pull_request` event and passes values through environment variables. It needs no access to the backlog.
- `fsck --code`, run by anyone from a machine that holds both clones, needs no credential. It lists commits on main with no declaration (admin merges, direct pushes), void closes, takeovers, claims on closed records and the skipped log lines. A scheduled audit is deferred: it needs a read credential for the backlog.

## 10. Readable view (optional, owner decision c)

- `basicly tracker board` and the CLI views read the machine clone.
- The event files are JSON lines, one event per line, with the record id and status in plain text, so a person can read them in the forge web UI.
- A team may add the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template to the backlog repository.

## 11. Migration and cutover

1. `migrate --to-backlog` imports the old ledger into an empty backlog, in today's fold order, before any clone attaches; the import is keyed by event id, so it resumes after a crash. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
2. The cutover PR adds `tracker.toml` and the README line, deletes `.basicly/ledger` and reinstalls the hook. Its check refuses while the old ledger holds events the backlog lacks.
3. After the cutover merges, the PR check refuses any PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` and names `migrate --to-backlog --branch`, which moves that branch's pending events and deletes its ledger changes. A revert of the cutover PR is refused by the same check; the undo is a forward PR that changes `tracker.toml`.
4. Every in-repo ledger command refuses when `tracker.toml` exists: "the tracker moved to <url>; run basicly tracker <command> without the ledger directory" (`commands.py:296-306` today creates the folder).
5. Guidance and skills that name `.basicly/ledger` (the workspace and project instruction files, the work-tracker skill) change with the release.

## 12. Kit changes

- New: `git_runner.py`, the one module that runs git, with argument lists only, and the revised `SPEC.md:154`; the machine clone, queue and share step; the ordered read layer with its cache; the declarations parser on top of `claims.py`; the code-history derivation; `attach`, `detach`, `claim --wait` and the exit codes; the PR check template; `migrate --to-backlog` and `--branch`.
- Replaced: the commit hook block (`claim_block.py`), `commit-check` (`cli.py:254-282`), the ledger location (`locate.py`, `commands.resolve_ledger`, `install_hook.py`).
- Changed: the fold gets the ordered mode and the claim rule inside `_hold`.
- Reused: event format and ids, `fsck.py`, `migrate.py`, `LedgerLock`, `holders.py`, the id parser in `claims.py`, `git_layout.git_dir`.
- A consumer with no basicly engine gets all of it from the tracker kit; the PR check ships as a CI template that calls the kit by path.

## 13. Removal

`basicly tracker detach` on each machine (it refuses while the queue holds unshared events, and names `share`); a code PR that deletes `.basicly/tracker.toml`, the README line, the PR check workflow and the hook block; archive or delete the backlog repository.

## 14. Proof tests

In CI on local bare repositories, except where named:
