# M5 design, version 3: the conflict-free tracker, core release

Record: basicly-gtb19bg.43. Study: basicly-gtb19bg.58. Design record: basicly-gtb19bg.60. Status: for owner approval; no code exists.

## 1. Requirement and decisions

Never-events (owner): N1, two open pull requests (PRs) edit the same tracker file and the second cannot merge; N2, agents on one machine overwrite each other, corrupt a file or need resolution work; N3, the tracker is out of sync with the code; N4, tracker state is not shared in time. Constraints: C2, no thousands of tracker files in the code repository; C3, nothing hidden (visible in the forge web UI, removable without inside knowledge; no git refs, no git notes).

Owner decisions of 2026-11-11: no tracker branch in the code repository; core first, hardening deferred; a readable `BACKLOG.md` is optional.

Kit rules this design changes, for owner approval: the tracker kit's `SPEC.md:154` (no network, no subprocess) and the kit boundary gate (`.basicly/core/hooks/kit-boundary.py:19`, which refuses `subprocess` in every kit). The design adds one module, `tracker/git_runner.py`, exempted by name in the gate, with a test that every other kit module is still refused.

## 2. Where the data lives

Backlog repository, `<code-repo>-backlog`, on the same forge:

- `log/<writer-id>.jsonl`: one append-only event file per writer. The first line is a header with the writer id, the display name and the author email the writer commits code with.
- `manifest.toml`: the normalized URL of the one code repository the backlog belongs to, and the format version.

Code repository: `.basicly/tracker.toml` with the backlog URL (the only tracker file, C2), and one README line with that URL (C3; the PR check refuses its absence).

## 3. The machine clone

- One backlog clone per machine, in the user state folder, named by a hash of the URL, mode 0700, outside every checkout; the read cache and the queue live inside its `.git` folder.
- Attaching needs read access, writing needs push rights; `attach` names what is missing and who grants it. With read access only, a developer commits code with `refs` and `none` declarations; claims and comments are refused by name.
- `attach` pins the backlog URL in the clone. Every command refuses a changed URL in `tracker.toml`: "the backlog URL changed from A to B; run basicly tracker attach B to accept". `attach` refuses a backlog whose `manifest.toml` names another code repository.
- Writer id: random, made once per clone, stored in `.git` with a hash of the machine id; a copied clone makes a new one.
- Session id: every process gets one. The holder of a claim is the pair (writer id, session id); the display name only labels it.
- Queue: `.git/basicly-queue.jsonl`. Under `LedgerLock`, a torn last line is cut back to the last newline before any read or append; a line that does not parse is kept, skipped and reported; rewrites go through a temporary file that replaces the queue.

## 4. Writing (N2)

- Event id: writer id plus a per-writer counter, kept in `.git`. Two events never share an id, so a new close from a stale clone is never mistaken for an old one (verified: the content-derived id of today's kit repeats in that case, `events.py:298-305`, `recurrence.py:94-119`). The in-repo ledger keeps content ids.
- Every write appends one event to the queue under `LedgerLock`, which covers only the queue file, then tries a share without waiting.

## 5. Sharing (N4)

One share attempt; no separate share lock:

1. `git fetch` the default branch.
2. Rewrite check: if the last seen tip is not an ancestor of the fetched head (any non-zero exit of `merge-base --is-ancestor`), refuse every share: "the backlog history was rewritten; events after <sha> are missing on the forge; run basicly tracker fsck". `fsck` also compares each writer's last pushed commit with the head, so the writer whose commits were dropped detects a rewrite that another reader cannot see.
3. Under `LedgerLock`, read the queue; release the lock.
4. Drop queued events whose ids are already in this writer's own file on the fetched head.
5. Build the commit with git plumbing outside the lock: a temporary index from the fetched head, the writer's own file with the queued events appended, `commit-tree` with the fetched head as the only parent.
6. `git push <commit>:<default branch>`, plain. On success, record the new tip and, under `LedgerLock`, remove the shared events from the queue by id.
7. On refusal, go to 1. After 5 attempts with random back-off, the events stay queued; each command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share" once, at the end.

Verified on local bare repositories (basicly-gtb19bg.58): this share kept 300 of 300 appends with no duplicates against concurrent pushers, three runs; a rebase-based share lost appends.

## 6. Reading and the claim rule

- The tool only ever pushes commits whose single parent is the head it fetched, so the default branch is a straight line. The read layer walks that line from the last cached commit. A commit with more than one parent (a merge pushed by plain git) is skipped, its lines are void, and `fsck` reports it with the command that re-shares those events. The cache is extended only when the old head is on the line; otherwise it is rebuilt.
- Lines that do not parse, lines changed after they were added and lines in a file whose header names another writer are void and reported.
- The fold gets an ordered mode for backlog ledgers: it keeps the input order, drops duplicate ids, and does not treat equal `seq` values as a fork; `seq` and the totals are computed from the order.
- Claim rule, in the fold: `_hold` returns a verdict for each claim event. In the ordered mode, the first open claim of a record wins; a later claim by any other (writer, session) is void, and the fold skips the field handler for a void claim, so a void claim never writes the holder (today the handler runs after `_hold` with no such check, `events.py:701-708`).

## 7. Claims

- Before a claim appends anything, the tool checks that the forge answers (`git ls-remote` with a 5 s timeout). Offline, it refuses and queues nothing: "claim needs the forge: run again when online".
- `claim <id>` then shares at once and waits with a 30 s deadline that kills any running git process. Exit codes: 0 claimed by this session; 3 held by another session ("held by <name> (<session>) since <time>; run basicly tracker claim <id> --take --reason <text> if the holder is gone"); 4 pending ("not yet on the forge; run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait").
- `--wait` blocks until the claim resolves or the deadline passes.
- A pending claim that lands later is reported by the next command of any session on that writer: "you hold <id> from session <s>; run basicly tracker release <id> if no one works on it".
- `claim --take` (exists, `arguments.py:241`) records a takeover event with a reason; `fsck` lists takeovers.
- Measured on local repositories with 8 agents: every claim within 4.1 s at 1 s latency; a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency gave a 26 s median with pending results. Contention is the main risk (section 15).

## 8. Closing a record from the code (N3)

- Declarations in commit messages: a record id at the end of the subject links (`refs`, as the commit hooks require today); `closes <id>` closes; `reopens <id>` reopens without reverting code; `none` marks work with no record. Several ids are allowed. The parser reads the whole message, indented lines included (a default `git merge --squash` indents the original messages), and is built on the existing id regex (`claims.py:31`, `:53-58`).
- Revert: a commit whose body says "This reverts commit <sha>" undoes the declarations of that commit only if <sha> is on the default branch and the revert's change is the inverse of that commit's change. Declarations inside the quoted subject `Revert "..."` are ignored. Any other revert text is void and reported.
- Order: effects apply where a commit enters the first-parent chain of the code default branch; the commits of a merged range apply at the merge commit, in their own order; the latest effect wins. A record closed by a backlog event and later named by code follows the same rule: the latest effect from either source wins.
- Who may close: a `closes` or `reopens` counts only if the commit's author email belongs to an attached writer (the header line in section 2) that held the record in the fold at the time of the commit. Otherwise it is void and `fsck --code` lists it. A fork contributor cannot close a record.
- Merge methods: the parser reads every commit reachable from the code default branch, so declarations survive squash with the default message, merge commits and rebase merges. The GitHub squash options "pull request title" and "pull request title and description" drop commit messages; the PR check therefore also requires the declaration in the PR title or description.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: refuses a missing declaration, a bare `closes` and an unknown id. Online, it fetches and refuses a `closes` from a non-holder. Offline, it allows the commit and prints that the close will be checked by `fsck --code`. When `tracker.toml` exists and no clone does, it refuses with "run basicly tracker attach <url>". Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m); a proof test installs it under a path with a double quote and `$(x)`. The hook block carries a version marker.
- Every command and the session start refuse when `tracker.toml` exists and the hook block lacks the current marker: "run basicly tracker install-hook".
- PR check (a CI template in the kit): it extracts the kit from the PR's base commit and runs that copy, so a PR cannot edit its own check. It refuses a PR with no declaration in its commits and in its title or description, a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` after cutover, a missing README line, and it flags any change to `tracker.toml`. It runs on the `pull_request` event, passes values through environment variables and needs no backlog access.
- `fsck --code`, from any machine with both clones and no credential: commits with no declaration (a merge commit whose range declares is exempt), void closes and reverts, takeovers, claims on closed records, skipped log lines and rewrites. A scheduled audit is deferred.
- `git_runner.py` validates every value before git sees it: a commit id against `^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$`, a writer id against a fixed pattern, a URL against `https://` and `ssh://` (and `file://` in tests); it puts `--end-of-options` before values and sets `protocol.allow=never` with only those protocols allowed. Text from events is stripped of control characters before any terminal or agent sees it.

## 10. Readable view (optional, owner decision c)

The board and CLI views read the machine clone. The event files are JSON lines with the record id and status in plain text, readable in the forge web UI. A team may add the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template to the backlog repository.

## 11. Migration and cutover

1. `migrate --to-backlog` imports the old ledger into an empty backlog, in today's fold order, keyed by event id, so it resumes after a crash. It refuses once any writer file exists. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
2. `migrate --verify` writes a digest of the old ledger and the backlog head into `.basicly/tracker.toml`. The cutover PR adds that file and the README line, deletes `.basicly/ledger` and reinstalls the hook. The PR check compares the digest with the old ledger in the PR's base commit and refuses on a mismatch, without backlog access.
3. After cutover, the PR check refuses a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` and names `migrate --to-backlog --branch`. That mode imports a branch's comments and notes, and lists its state changes (status, claims) for a person to re-enter; it never replays an old state change after newer ones. A revert of the cutover is refused by the same check; the undo is a forward PR.
4. Every in-repo ledger command refuses when `tracker.toml` exists: "the tracker moved to <url>; run the command without the ledger directory" (`commands.py:296-306` today creates the folder).

## 12. Kit and engine changes, and build order

- New in the kit (about 8): `git_runner.py`; attach, clone and queue; the share step; the ordered read layer with its cache; the declarations parser; the code-history derivation; `claim --wait` and exit codes; the PR check template.
- Replaced (4): the hook block (`claim_block.py`), `commit-check` (`cli.py:254-282`), `locate.py`, the ledger part of `install_hook.py`.
- Changed: `events.py` (ordered mode, writer ids, the claim verdict), `forks.py`, `fsck.py`, `migrate.py`, the 27 `directory` arguments in `arguments.py`.
- Outside the kit: 60 files and 168 lines in `src`, `tests` and `.basicly/core/hooks` name `.basicly/ledger`. One storage resolver in the kit returns the in-repo ledger or the machine clone; every reader calls it.
- Guidance and skills that name `.basicly/ledger` change with the release.
- Build order, each slice shipped behind `tracker.toml` so the in-repo ledger keeps working: S1 `git_runner.py`, the gate exemption and the SPEC line; S2 the ordered fold, writer ids and the claim verdict; S3 attach, queue, share and read layer (the riskiest slice: a contention probe on a sandbox forge runs first); S4 claims and exit codes; S5 the declarations parser and `fsck --code`, read-only, useful on today's ledger; S6 the hook and the PR check; S7 migration, cutover, the resolver sweep and the sandbox proofs.

## 13. Removal

`detach` on each machine (refuses while the queue holds unshared events and names `share`); a code PR deleting `tracker.toml`, the README line, the PR check workflow and the hook block; archive or delete the backlog repository.

## 14. Proof tests

On local bare repositories in CI, except where named:

- N1: 1000 tracker writes leave `git status --porcelain` empty in the code repository. On sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories at release: two code PRs that ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees write 1000 events against a remote with 1 s push latency; every event lands once; no `LedgerLock` wait above 1 s; a kill after the push and before the queue clear causes no duplicate; a torn queue tail is repaired; a copied clone gets a new writer id; a stale clone's second close is not dropped.
- N3: two `refs` commits keep a record open; `closes` closes it; its git default revert reopens it and is not read as a close; the revert of that revert closes it; `reopens` reopens it; a fake revert message and a `closes` by an author who is not an attached holder are void; a direct push without a declaration is listed by `fsck --code`. Locally: `git merge --squash` with the default message, a merge commit and a rebase keep the declaration. On the sandbox forges: each squash setting.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones and 8 sessions in one clone claim one record, and exactly one session gets exit code 0; a claim pushed by plain git as a merge is void; a pending claim resolves to one holder; a force-pushed backlog makes shares refuse; an offline claim queues nothing.
- Migration: killed at each step it resumes to equal records; a re-import after a writer file exists is refused; an in-repo command after cutover refuses by name.
- Security: hostile values (a commit id with `-`, a URL starting with `-`, a writer id with `/`) are refused by `git_runner.py`; the hook path test above.

## 15. Deferred, open, and owner actions

- Deferred (owner decision b): identity binding beyond the author email header, commit signing, CODEOWNERS, `attach --restore`, claim expiry, the backlog pre-push hook, the scheduled audit, one backlog for several code repositories, a required `BACKLOG.md`.
- Open: contention on a real forge (if claims stay pending too long, comments and fields move to one branch per writer and only claims, releases and closes stay on the default branch); Bitbucket's squash default (not documented).
- Owner actions: approve the kit rule change in section 1; approve provisioning sandbox repositories on GitHub and Bitbucket with a scoped token as a CI secret for the release proofs.

## 3. The machine clone

- One backlog clone per machine, in the user state folder, named by a hash of the URL, mode 0700, outside every checkout; the queue, the read cache and the last seen tip live in its `.git` folder.
- `attach <url>` clones, pins the URL, writes the writer header and installs the hook in one step. It refuses a backlog whose `manifest.toml` names another code URL than the one in `tracker.toml`. It refuses while another clone for the same code repository still holds queued events, and names `basicly tracker share --clone <path>`.
- Access: reading needs read access, writing needs push rights; `attach` names what is missing and who grants it. Without read access (a fork contributor), `attach --contributor` records contributor mode: the hook checks only the declaration syntax, and tracker writes are refused by name.
- Writer id: random, made once per clone with a hash of the machine id; a copied clone makes a new one.
- Session id: the agent's host sets `BASICLY_SESSION` for the whole agent session (in Claude Code, the basicly session-start hook writes it; the mechanism is to be verified against the vendor docs, section 15); a person or another host passes `--session <id>`. A claim with no session id is refused by name. The holder of a claim is (writer id, session id); the display name only labels it.

## 4. Writing (N2)

- Event id: the writer id plus a random 128-bit value, assigned when the event enters the queue and stored with it. A re-send keeps its id, so duplicates are dropped; no counter exists, so nothing can roll back and reuse an id (removes the v3 counter and its loss case).
- Every write appends one event to the queue under `LedgerLock`, which covers only the queue file, then tries a share without waiting.
- Queue file: a torn last line is cut back to the last newline under `LedgerLock` before any read or append; an unparseable line is kept, skipped and reported; rewrites go through a temporary file that replaces the queue.

## 5. Sharing (N4)

A share lock per clone (restored; v2 removed it and caused false rewrite refusals) serializes shares; a command that does not need the result skips the share if the lock is taken.

Under the share lock:

1. `git fetch` the default branch into a ref owned by this clone.
2. Rewrite check: if the last seen tip is not an ancestor of the fetched head, refuse: "the backlog history was rewritten; run basicly tracker fsck --repair". `fsck --repair` finds this writer's events at its last pushed commit (kept alive by a local tag), queues the missing ones, and accepts the new head.
3. Under `LedgerLock`, read the queue.
4. Drop queued events whose ids are valid events on the fetched head.
5. Build the commit with git plumbing: a temporary index from the fetched head, this writer's file with the queued events appended, `commit-tree` with the fetched head as the only parent.
6. `git push <commit>:<default branch>`, plain. On success, write the last seen tip and the local tag, and under `LedgerLock` remove the shared events from the queue by id.
7. On refusal, go to 1; after 5 attempts with random back-off the events stay queued, and each command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share" once, at the end.

- The tool only pushes commits whose single parent is the fetched head, so the branch is a straight line. The read layer walks it from the last cached commit; a commit with more than one parent (a merge pushed by plain git) is skipped and its lines are void; `fsck` names `basicly tracker share --reissue <commit>`, which gives those events new ids and queues them.
- Lines that do not parse, lines changed after they were added and lines in a file whose header names another writer are void and reported.
- The fold gets an ordered mode for backlog ledgers: input order kept, duplicate ids dropped, equal `seq` values not a fork; `seq` and totals computed from the order.
- Holder verdict for every event that changes the holder, not only claims: a claim when the record is held by another session is void; an `unassign` is valid only from the holder or with `--take`; a take is valid and logged. The fold skips the field handler for a void event, so a void event never writes the holder. (Today `unassign` checks nothing, basicly-qtmesvv.)
- Migrated holders that are person names stay as legacy holders; a claim by any session on such a record is void until the person unassigns it or someone takes it.

## 7. Claims

- Before a claim appends anything, the tool checks that the forge answers (`git ls-remote`, 5 s). Offline, it refuses and queues nothing.
- `claim <id>` shares at once and waits, 30 s, killing any running git process at the deadline. Exit codes: 0 claimed by this session; 3 held by another session ("held by <name> since <time>; run basicly tracker claim <id> --take if the holder is gone"); 4 pending ("run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait"); 5 offline; 6 `--wait` ran out of time.
- A pending claim that lands later is reported by the next command of the same session; release with `basicly tracker unassign <id>`.
- Measured on local repositories with 8 agents: every claim within 4.1 s at 1 s latency; a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency gave a 26 s median with pending results. Contention is the main open risk (section 15).

## 8. Closing a record from the code (N3)

- Source rule (restored from v2): a record with linked commits closes and reopens only from the code; a backlog `close` is for records with no code. There is no cross-repository ordering.
- Declarations in commit messages: a record id at the end of the subject links (`refs`), as the hooks require today; `closes <id>` closes; `reopens <id>` reopens; `none` marks work with no record. Several ids are allowed. One parser, built on the existing id regex (`claims.py:31`, `:53-58`), used by the hook, the PR check and the derivation. It refuses close-like words that are not exactly `closes` (`close`, `fixes`, `resolves`, `Closes`) by name.
- Who may close: anyone whose commit reaches the default branch. The merge into main is the authorization, the same trust as the code itself (removes the v3 author-holder rule). `fsck --code` lists every close with its commit. Risk, deferred hardening: a maintainer merges a fork PR without reading its commit messages.
- Order: effects apply where a commit enters the first-parent chain of the code default branch; a merged range applies at its merge commit, in commit order; inside a squash message, the lines apply in their own order, so an indented revert after an indented `closes` cancels it. Latest effect wins.
- Revert: "This reverts commit <sha>" undoes that commit's declarations when <sha> is on the default branch or named earlier in the same squash message. Declarations inside a quoted `Revert "..."` subject are ignored.
- Merge methods: every commit reachable from the default branch is read, so declarations survive the default squash, merge commits and rebase merges. The GitHub squash options "pull request title" and "pull request title and description" drop commit messages, so the PR check requires the declaration in the PR title.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: refuses a missing or malformed declaration and an unknown id; in contributor mode it checks syntax only. When `tracker.toml` exists and no clone does, it refuses with "run basicly tracker attach <url>" (or `--contributor`). Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m). The hook block carries a version marker; every command refuses a stale block and names `basicly tracker install-hook`.
- PR check (CI template): extracts the kit from the PR's base commit and runs that copy. It requires one declaration in the PR title and, for each commit, a declaration or none; refuses a PR touching `.basicly/ledger` after cutover; refuses a missing README line; flags any change to `tracker.toml`; is skipped entirely for a PR that deletes `tracker.toml` (removal). It runs on `pull_request` and passes values through environment variables.
- Required status check: marking the PR check required on the default branch is an owner step of the cutover (section 11), stated in the kit's setup.
- `fsck --code` runs incrementally inside session start and every tracker command, from the last checked code commit, and prints each new void declaration with its next action. No credential is needed. A scheduled audit is deferred.
- `git_runner.py` validates values before git sees them (commit ids against `^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$`, writer ids against a fixed pattern, URLs against `https://` and `ssh://`, `file://` in tests), puts `--end-of-options` before values and allows only those protocols. Event text is stripped of control characters before a terminal or agent sees it.

## 10. Readable view (optional)

The board and CLI views read the machine clone; event lines are JSON with the record id and status in plain text; a team may add the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template.

## 11. Migration and cutover

1. `migrate --to-backlog` imports the old ledger into the backlog as the migration writer, in today's fold order, keyed by event id; it resumes after a crash by skipping ids already imported, and refuses if any writer file other than its own exists. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
2. `migrate --verify` writes a digest of the old ledger and the backlog head into `tracker.toml`; the cutover PR adds that file and the README line, deletes `.basicly/ledger` and reinstalls the hook. The PR check compares the digest with the old ledger in the base commit; on a mismatch it names `migrate --to-backlog` then `migrate --verify`.
3. Owner step: mark the PR check as a required status check.
4. After cutover, a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` is refused with `migrate --to-backlog --branch`, which imports the branch's comments and notes, lists its state changes for a person to re-enter, and then deletes the branch's ledger changes in one commit on that branch, so the PR passes. A revert of the cutover is refused; the undo is a forward PR.
5. Every in-repo ledger command refuses when `tracker.toml` exists: "the tracker moved to <url>; run the command without the ledger directory".

## 12. Changes and build order

- New in the kit (about 8): `git_runner.py`; attach, clone and queue; the share step; the ordered read layer; the declarations parser; the code-history derivation; claim exit codes and `--wait`; the PR check template.
- Replaced (4): the hook block, `commit-check` (`cli.py:254-282`), `locate.py`, the ledger part of `install_hook.py`.
- Changed: `events.py` (ordered mode, holder verdicts), `forks.py`, `fsck.py`, `migrate.py`, the 27 `directory` arguments.
- Outside the kit: 60 files and 168 lines in `src`, `tests` and `.basicly/core/hooks` name `.basicly/ledger`; one storage resolver in the kit serves them all. Guidance and skills change with the release.
- Build order, each slice behind `tracker.toml` so the in-repo ledger keeps working: S1 `git_runner.py` and the gate exemption; S2 ordered fold and holder verdicts (also fixes basicly-qtmesvv for today's ledger); S3 attach, queue, share, read layer (riskiest: a contention probe on a sandbox forge first); S4 claims; S5 parser and `fsck --code`, read-only and useful on today's ledger; S6 hook and PR check; S7 migration, cutover, resolver sweep, sandbox proofs.

## 13. Removal

`detach` on each machine (refuses while the queue holds unshared events); one code PR deleting `tracker.toml`, the README line, the PR check workflow and the hook block (the PR check skips such a PR); the owner removes the required status check; archive or delete the backlog repository.

## 14. Proof tests

On local bare repositories in CI, except where named:

- N1: 1000 tracker writes leave `git status --porcelain` empty in the code repository; on sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories at release, two code PRs that ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees write 1000 events against a remote with 1 s push latency; every event lands once; no `LedgerLock` wait above 1 s; two sessions share at once with no false rewrite refusal; a kill after the push and before the queue clear causes no duplicate; a torn queue tail is repaired; a copied clone gets a new writer id.
- N3: `refs` keeps a record open; `closes` closes it; its default revert reopens it and is not read as a close; the revert of that revert closes it; `reopens` reopens it; a squash with an in-branch close and revert leaves it open; `fixes <id>` is refused by the hook; a direct push without a declaration is listed by the incremental `fsck --code`; a backlog close on a record with code is refused.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones and 8 sessions in one clone claim one record and exactly one session gets exit 0; an `unassign` by a non-holder is void; a claim pushed by plain git as a merge is void and `--reissue` restores its events; a pending claim resolves to one holder; a force-push makes shares refuse and `fsck --repair` restores this writer's events; an offline claim queues nothing.
- Migration: killed at each step it resumes to equal records; a legacy name holder blocks claims until unassigned; an in-repo command after cutover refuses by name; `--branch` leaves the branch mergeable.
- Security: hostile values are refused by `git_runner.py`; the hook installed under a path with a double quote and `$(x)` runs nothing.

## 15. Deferred, open, owner actions

- Deferred (owner decision b): identity binding (author checks, signing), CODEOWNERS, `attach --restore` beyond `fsck --repair`, claim expiry, the backlog pre-push hook, the scheduled audit, one backlog for several code repositories, a required `BACKLOG.md`. Named risk: a fork PR merged unread can close a record.
- Open: contention on a real forge (fallback: comments and fields on one branch per writer, claims and closes on the default branch); Bitbucket's squash default (not documented); how Claude Code lets a session-start hook set `BASICLY_SESSION` for later commands (check the vendor docs before S4).
- Owner actions: approve the kit rule change (section 1); approve sandbox repositories on GitHub and Bitbucket with a scoped token as a CI secret; mark the PR check required at cutover.

# M5 design, version 5: the conflict-free tracker, core release

Record: basicly-gtb19bg.43. Study: basicly-gtb19bg.58. Design record: basicly-gtb19bg.60. Status: for owner approval; no code exists. Version 4 removed mechanisms that versions 2 and 3 added. Version 5 answers the 7 blockers of the third climb round, again by removing rules where it can: no revert inference, `refs` never changes status, one conflict model.

## 1. Requirement and decisions

Never-events (owner): N1, two open pull requests (PRs) edit the same tracker file and the second cannot merge; N2, agents on one machine overwrite each other, corrupt a file or need resolution work; N3, the tracker is out of sync with the code; N4, tracker state is not shared in time. Constraints: C2, no thousands of tracker files in the code repository; C3, nothing hidden (visible in the forge web UI, removable without inside knowledge; no git refs, no git notes).

Owner decisions of 2026-11-11: no tracker branch in the code repository; core first, hardening deferred; a readable `BACKLOG.md` is optional.

Kit rules this design changes, for owner approval: `SPEC.md:154` (no network, no subprocess) and the kit boundary gate (`.basicly/core/hooks/kit-boundary.py:19`, which refuses `subprocess` in every kit). One module, `tracker/git_runner.py`, is exempted by name, with a test that every other kit module is still refused.

## 2. Where the data lives

- Backlog repository `<code-repo>-backlog` on the same forge: `log/<writer-id>.jsonl`, one append-only event file per writer, whose first line names the writer and its display name (N1, N2: no two writers touch one file, so even a writer who bypasses the tool with `git pull --rebase` cannot conflict); `manifest.toml` with the code repository URL and the format version.
- Code repository: `.basicly/tracker.toml` with the backlog URL (the only tracker file, C2) and one README line with that URL (C3).

## 3. The machine clone

- One backlog clone per machine, in the user state folder, named by a hash of the URL, mode 0700, outside every checkout; the queue, the read cache and the last seen tip live in its `.git` folder.
- `attach <url>` clones, pins the URL, writes the writer header and installs the hook in one step. It refuses a backlog whose `manifest.toml` names another code URL than the one in `tracker.toml`. It refuses while another clone for the same code repository still holds queued events, and names `basicly tracker detach <path>`, which shares that queue first.
- Access: reading needs read access, writing needs push rights; `attach` names what is missing and who grants it. Without read access (a fork contributor), `attach --contributor` records contributor mode: the hook checks only the declaration syntax, and tracker writes are refused by name.
- Writer id: random, made once per clone with a hash of the machine id; a copied clone makes a new one.
- Session id: in Claude Code, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, which the host already sets for Bash commands (vendor docs: it changes on `/clear`, and subagents share it, so one Claude session is one holder and `/clear` starts a new holder). Another host or a person runs `basicly tracker session new`, which mints a random id registered in the clone; `--session` accepts only an id this clone minted or the host variable. A claim with no session id is refused by name. The holder of a claim is (writer id, session id).
- Display name: `BASICLY_HOLDER` and `git config basicly.holder` (`holders.py:34-38`, `:81`) supply only the display name of a holder, never the identity.

## 4. Writing (N2)

- Event id: the writer id plus a random 128-bit value, assigned when the event enters the queue and stored with it. A re-send keeps its id, so duplicates are dropped; no counter exists, so nothing can roll back and reuse an id (removes the v3 counter and its loss case).
- Every write appends one event to the queue under `LedgerLock`, which covers only the queue file, then tries a share without waiting.
- Queue file: a torn last line is cut back to the last newline under `LedgerLock` before any read or append; an unparseable line is kept, skipped and reported; rewrites go through a temporary file that replaces the queue.

## 5. Sharing (N4)

A share lock per clone (restored; v2 removed it and caused false rewrite refusals) serializes shares; a command that does not need the result skips the share if the lock is taken.

Under the share lock:

1. `git fetch` the default branch into a ref owned by this clone.
2. Rewrite check: if the last seen tip is not an ancestor of the fetched head, refuse: "the backlog history was rewritten; run basicly tracker fsck --repair". `fsck --repair` finds this writer's events at its last pushed commit (kept alive by a local tag), queues the missing ones, and accepts the new head.
3. Under `LedgerLock`, read the queue.
4. Drop queued events whose ids are anywhere on the fetched head, valid or void. If an id appears twice in the log, the fold keeps the first copy, so a crash can never bring a void claim back.
5. Build the commit with git plumbing: a temporary index from the fetched head, this writer's file with the queued events appended, `commit-tree` with the fetched head as the only parent.
6. `git push <commit>:<default branch>`, plain. On success, write the last seen tip and the local tag, and under `LedgerLock` remove the shared events from the queue by id. If the queue still holds events (written during the push by commands that skipped the busy share lock), go to step 1 before releasing the share lock, so no event is left without a sharer.
7. On refusal, go to 1; after 5 attempts with random back-off the events stay queued, and each command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share" once, at the end.

Verified on local bare repositories (basicly-gtb19bg.58): this share kept 300 of 300 appends with no duplicates against concurrent pushers; a rebase-based share lost appends.

## 6. Reading and holder verdicts

- The tool only pushes commits whose single parent is the fetched head, so the branch is a straight line. The read layer walks it from the last cached commit; a commit with more than one parent (a merge pushed by plain git), a deleted or renamed writer file and a changed line are void; `fsck --repair` gives the void events of this writer new ids and queues them (one repair command for rewrites and void merges).
- Lines that do not parse, lines changed after they were added and lines in a file whose header names another writer are void and reported.
- The fold gets an ordered mode for backlog ledgers: input order kept, duplicate ids dropped, equal `seq` values not a fork; `seq` and totals computed from the order; for an id that appears twice, the first copy counts.
- Holder verdict for every event that changes the holder, not only claims: a claim when the record is held by another session is void; an `unassign` is valid only from the holder or with `--take`; a take is valid and logged. The fold skips the field handler for a void event, so a void event never writes the holder. (Today `unassign` checks nothing, basicly-qtmesvv.)
- One conflict model: in the ordered mode the holder verdicts replace the `contested` state (`events.py:609-611`), the fork findings of `forks.py` and the `resolve` command (`arguments.py:243`); on a backlog ledger `resolve` refuses by name, because nothing is left to resolve.
- Migrated holders that are person names stay as legacy holders. An `unassign` is valid when the display name of the writer equals the legacy name; a claim by any session on such a record is void until that unassign or a take.

## 7. Claims

- Before a claim appends anything, the tool checks that the forge answers (`git ls-remote`, 5 s). Offline, it refuses and queues nothing.
- `claim <id>` shares at once and waits, 30 s, killing any running git process at the deadline. Exit codes: 0 claimed by this session; 3 held by another session ("held by <name> since <time>; run basicly tracker claim <id> --take if the holder is gone"); 4 pending, also when `--wait` runs out of time ("run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait"); 5 offline.
- A pending claim that lands later is reported by the next command of the same session; release with `basicly tracker unassign <id>`.
- Measured on local repositories with 8 agents: every claim within 4.1 s at 1 s latency; a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency gave a 26 s median with pending results. Contention is the main open risk (section 15).

## 8. Closing a record from the code (N3)

- Only two declarations change status: `closes <id>` and `reopens <id>`. A record id at the end of the subject (`refs`, as the hooks require today) only links a commit to a record and never changes its status; `none` marks work with no record. One parser, built on the existing id regex (`claims.py:31`, `:53-58`), used by the hook, the PR check and the derivation. It refuses close-like words that are not exactly `closes` (`close`, `fixes`, `resolves`, `Closes`) by name.
- Source rule: a record that has ever had a code `closes` or `reopens` changes status only from the code; a backlog `close` or reopen on such a record is refused by name. A record with only `refs` links, or with no code, closes and reopens in the backlog. A later `refs` therefore never reopens a backlog-closed record.
- No revert inference (removes three round 3 defects: squash and rebase do not keep the reverted commit id on main, a merge revert carries only the merge message, and `git merge --squash` lists the revert before the close). Declarations inside a quoted `Revert "..."` subject are ignored, so a default git revert and a forge Revert button carry no declaration; the hook and the PR check refuse them until the author adds `reopens <id>` (or `none`). A person who reverts a close says so.
- One commit that declares both `closes <id>` and `reopens <id>` (for example a squash of a branch that closed and then reverted) has no effect on that id; `fsck --code` lists it. This is the right net result whatever order the squash message uses.
- Who may close: anyone whose commit reaches the default branch; the merge into main is the authorization, the same trust as the code itself. `fsck --code` lists every close with its commit. Named risk, deferred hardening: a maintainer merges a fork PR without reading its commit messages.
- Order: effects apply where a commit enters the first-parent chain of the code default branch; a merged range applies at its merge commit; the latest effect wins.
- Merge methods: every commit reachable from the default branch is read, so declarations survive the default squash, merge commits and rebase merges. The GitHub squash options "pull request title" and "pull request title and description" drop commit messages, so the PR check requires the declaration in the PR title as well.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: refuses a missing or malformed declaration and an unknown id; in contributor mode it checks syntax only. When `tracker.toml` exists and no clone does, it refuses with "run basicly tracker attach <url>" (or `--contributor`). Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m). The hook block carries a version marker; every command and the session start refuse a stale block and name `basicly tracker install-hook`.
- The old hook block runs only while `.basicly/ledger` exists (`claim_block.py:57`), so after cutover it checks nothing. Therefore the new hook block ships in a release before cutover and works with the in-repo ledger too; the cutover runs only after every developer's session start has installed it. A machine that skipped it is caught by the PR check and by `fsck --code`.
- PR check (CI template): extracts the kit from the PR's base commit and runs that copy. It requires a declaration in the PR title and, for each commit, a declaration or `none`; refuses a PR touching `.basicly/ledger` after cutover; refuses a missing README line; refuses any change to the backlog URL in `tracker.toml` (moving a backlog is deferred). A removal PR is recognised only when it changes exactly the removal set (`tracker.toml`, the README line, the PR check workflow); a deletion of `tracker.toml` mixed with other changes is refused by name. It runs on `pull_request` and passes values through environment variables.
- Required status check: the owner marks the PR check required at cutover. Enforcement depends on the plan: GitHub enforces it for public repositories on GitHub Free and for all repositories on Pro, Team and Enterprise; Bitbucket only warns without Premium (vendor docs). Where it is not enforced, the PR check advises and `fsck --code` at every session start reports every merge that bypassed a refusal. The kit states this guarantee per plan.
- `fsck --code` runs incrementally inside session start and every tracker command, from the last checked code commit, and prints each new void declaration with its next action. No credential is needed. A scheduled audit is deferred.
- `git_runner.py` validates values before git sees them (commit ids against `^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$`, writer ids against a fixed pattern, URLs against `https://` and `ssh://`, `file://` in tests), puts `--end-of-options` before values and allows only those protocols. Event text is stripped of control characters before a terminal or agent sees it.

## 10. Readable view (optional)

The board and CLI views read the machine clone; event lines are JSON with the record id and status in plain text; a team may add the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template.

## 11. Migration and cutover

0. Before cutover: the release with the new hook block is installed on every machine (section 9).
1. `migrate --freeze` writes a marker into the old ledger; from then on every in-repo write refuses with "the tracker is moving to a backlog; wait for the cutover". Nothing new enters the old ledger, so the import cannot fall behind.
2. `migrate --to-backlog` imports the frozen ledger into an empty backlog as the migration writer, in today's fold order, keyed by event id; it resumes after a crash by skipping ids already imported, and refuses if any writer file other than its own exists. Nobody attaches before the cutover merges, so no other writer file can exist. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
3. `migrate --verify` writes a digest of the frozen ledger and the backlog head into `tracker.toml`; the cutover PR adds that file and the README line and deletes `.basicly/ledger`. The PR check compares the digest with the frozen ledger in the base commit; on a mismatch it names `migrate --to-backlog` then `migrate --verify`, which can always run again because the ledger is frozen.
4. Owner step: mark the PR check as a required status check where the plan allows.
5. After cutover, a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` is refused with `migrate --to-backlog --branch`, which imports the branch's comments and notes, lists its state changes for a person to re-enter, and then deletes the branch's ledger changes in one commit on that branch, so the PR passes. A revert of the cutover is refused; the undo is a forward PR.
6. Every in-repo ledger command refuses when `tracker.toml` exists: "the tracker moved to <url>; run the command without the ledger directory".

## 12. Changes and build order

- New in the kit (about 8): `git_runner.py`; attach, clone and queue; the share step; the ordered read layer; the declarations parser; the code-history derivation; claim exit codes and `--wait`; the PR check template.
- Replaced (4): the hook block, `commit-check` (`cli.py:254-282`), `locate.py`, the ledger part of `install_hook.py`.
- Changed: `events.py` (ordered mode, holder verdicts), `fsck.py`, `migrate.py` (freeze, import, verify), the 28 `directory` arguments. Replaced on backlog ledgers: the `contested` state, the fork findings of `forks.py` and the `resolve` command, which refuses by name.
- Outside the kit: 60 files and 168 lines in `src`, `tests` and `.basicly/core/hooks` name `.basicly/ledger`; one storage resolver in the kit serves them all. Guidance and skills change with the release.
- Build order, each slice behind `tracker.toml` so the in-repo ledger keeps working: S1 `git_runner.py` and the gate exemption; S2 ordered fold and holder verdicts (also fixes basicly-qtmesvv for today's ledger); S3 attach, queue, share, read layer (riskiest: a contention probe on a sandbox forge first); S4 claims; S5 parser and `fsck --code`, read-only and useful on today's ledger; S6 hook and PR check; S7 migration, cutover, resolver sweep, sandbox proofs.

## 13. Removal

In this order: the owner removes the required status check; `detach` on each machine (it shares the queue first and removes the hook block); one code PR that changes exactly the removal set, `tracker.toml`, the README line and the PR check workflow (the PR check recognises that set and passes it); archive or delete the backlog repository. `basicly tracker remove` prints these steps.

## 14. Proof tests

On local bare repositories in CI, except where named:

- N1: 1000 tracker writes leave `git status --porcelain` empty in the code repository; on sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories at release, two code PRs that ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees write 1000 events against a remote with 1 s push latency; every event lands once; no `LedgerLock` wait above 1 s; two sessions share at once with no false rewrite refusal; a kill after the push and before the queue clear causes no duplicate; a torn queue tail is repaired; a copied clone gets a new writer id.
- N3: `refs` never changes status, also after a backlog close; `closes` closes; `reopens` reopens; a default git revert with no declaration is refused by the hook and by the PR check, and accepted after `reopens <id>` is added; a squash whose message declares both `closes` and `reopens` for one id leaves its status unchanged, in either line order; `fixes <id>` is refused; a direct push without a declaration is listed by the incremental `fsck --code`; a backlog close on a record with a code close is refused. Each case under squash, merge-commit and rebase merges on local repositories; the forge squash settings on the sandbox forges.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones and 8 sessions in one clone claim one record and exactly one session gets exit 0; an `unassign` by a non-holder is void; a claim pushed by plain git as a merge is void and `fsck --repair` restores its events; a pending claim resolves to one holder; a void claim re-sent after a crash stays void; an event written while the share lock was busy is shared before the lock is released; a force-push makes shares refuse and `fsck --repair` restores this writer's events; an offline claim queues nothing; two processes that pass one literal `--session` value are refused.
- Migration: killed at each step it resumes to equal records; an in-repo write after `migrate --freeze` is refused; a digest mismatch is repaired by running import and verify again; a legacy name holder is released by an `unassign` from that name; an in-repo command after cutover refuses by name; `--branch` leaves the branch mergeable.
- Removal: a PR that deletes `tracker.toml` together with other files is refused; the exact removal set passes; a PR that changes the backlog URL is refused.
- Security: hostile values are refused by `git_runner.py`; the hook installed under a path with a double quote and `$(x)` runs nothing.

## 15. Deferred, open, owner actions

- Deferred (owner decision b): identity binding (author checks, signing), CODEOWNERS, `attach --restore` beyond `fsck --repair`, claim expiry, the backlog pre-push hook, the scheduled audit, one backlog for several code repositories, a required `BACKLOG.md`. Named risk: a fork PR merged unread can close a record.
- Deferred as well: moving a backlog to a new URL.
- Open: contention on a real forge (fallback: comments and fields on one branch per writer, claims and closes on the default branch); Bitbucket's squash default (not documented); whether `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` reaches the Bash commands of subagents (vendor docs say subagents share the session; to test before S4).
- Owner actions: approve the kit rule change (section 1); approve sandbox repositories on GitHub and Bitbucket with a scoped token as a CI secret; mark the PR check required at cutover where the plan allows.

## 16. Changes from version 4

| Round 3 blocker | Answer in version 5 |
| --- | --- |
| Reverts matched by commit id | No revert inference; a revert carries `reopens <id>`; both in one commit cancel (section 8) |
| `refs` reopens a backlog-closed record | `refs` never changes status; source rule keyed on a code close (section 8) |
| Stranded event, void claim re-pushed | Share loops until the queue is empty; ids anywhere on the head are dropped; first copy wins (section 5) |
| Legacy hold, digest mismatch | Unassign by the legacy name; `migrate --freeze` before import (sections 6, 11) |
| Removal bypass, URL change | Exact removal set; URL change refused; removal order (sections 9, 13) |
| Old hook after cutover | New hook ships and installs before cutover (sections 9, 11) |
| Two conflict models | Holder verdicts replace contested, forks and resolve (sections 6, 12) |
| Session identity | `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, or ids minted by `session new` (section 3) |
| Required check per plan | Guarantee stated per plan; `fsck --code` reports bypasses (section 9) |

payload.text: [check of v5 2026-11-11, 3 Opus lenses] Of the 9 blockers in section 16, the lenses count resolved: recovery 7, misuse 6, correctness 7. Still open: (1) code close derivation: a squash of close, revert with reopens, close again declares both and gives no effect though the net intent is closed (ran, git merge --squash); a squash of a revert-only branch carries the quoted revert in the body, so its closes counts (ran); a forge Revert-button PR may carry none and leave the record closed; (2) session identity: parallel subagents share CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID and both get exit 0, and no mechanism detects a reused --session value; (3) cutover gate: nothing observes that every machine installed the new hook, branches cut before the freeze can still merge ledger writes, the freeze has no undo; (4) share drain loop is unbounded under a steady append stream; (5) fsck --repair could re-queue a claim voided by the holder rule; (6) removal: half-done removal has no state, and a PR can edit its own workflow file (forge behaviour unverified); (7) the read rule for status when a stale writer pushes a backlog close after a code reopen is unstated. Pattern: four of five design rounds put the largest open set in the code-close derivation from commit messages.

## 1. Requirement and decisions

Never-events (owner): N1, two open pull requests (PRs) edit the same tracker file and the second cannot merge; N2, agents on one machine overwrite each other, corrupt a file or need resolution work; N3, the tracker is out of sync with the code; N4, tracker state is not shared in time. Constraints: C2, no thousands of tracker files in the code repository; C3, nothing hidden (visible in the forge web UI, removable without inside knowledge; no git refs, no git notes).

Owner decisions of 2026-11-11: no tracker branch in the code repository; core first, hardening deferred; a readable `BACKLOG.md` is optional.

Kit rules this design changes, for owner approval: `SPEC.md:154` (no network, no subprocess) and the kit boundary gate (`.basicly/core/hooks/kit-boundary.py:19`, which refuses `subprocess` in every kit). One module, `tracker/git_runner.py`, is exempted by name, with a test that every other kit module is still refused.

## 2. Where the data lives

- Backlog repository `<code-repo>-backlog` on the same forge: `log/<writer-id>.jsonl`, one append-only event file per writer, whose first line names the writer and its display name (N1, N2: no two writers touch one file, so even a writer who bypasses the tool with `git pull --rebase` cannot conflict); `manifest.toml` with the code repository URL and the format version.
- Code repository: `.basicly/tracker.toml` with the backlog URL (the only tracker file, C2) and one README line with that URL (C3).

## 3. The machine clone

- One backlog clone per machine, in the user state folder, named by a hash of the URL, mode 0700, outside every checkout; the queue, the read cache and the last seen tip live in its `.git` folder.
- `attach <url>` clones, pins the URL, writes the writer header and installs the hook in one step. It refuses a backlog whose `manifest.toml` names another code URL than the one in `tracker.toml`. It refuses while another clone for the same code repository still holds queued events, and names `basicly tracker detach <path>`, which shares that queue first.
- Access: reading needs read access, writing needs push rights; `attach` names what is missing and who grants it. Without read access (a fork contributor), `attach --contributor` records contributor mode: the hook checks only the declaration syntax, and tracker writes are refused by name.
- Writer id: random, made once per clone with a hash of the machine id; a copied clone makes a new one.
- Session id: in Claude Code, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, which the host already sets for Bash commands (vendor docs: it changes on `/clear`, and subagents share it). One Claude session is one holder (owner decision): the agent that claims a record does the work or hands it to its own subagents. Another host or a person runs `basicly tracker session new`, which mints a random id registered in the clone; one id is one worker, and `--session` accepts only an id this clone minted or the host variable. A claim with no session id is refused by name. The holder of a claim is (writer id, session id).
- Display name: `BASICLY_HOLDER` and `git config basicly.holder` (`holders.py:34-38`, `:81`) supply only the display name of a holder, never the identity.

## 4. Writing (N2)

- Event id: the writer id plus a random 128-bit value, assigned when the event enters the queue and stored with it. A re-send keeps its id, so duplicates are dropped; no counter exists, so nothing can roll back and reuse an id (removes the v3 counter and its loss case).
- Every write appends one event to the queue under `LedgerLock`, which covers only the queue file, then tries a share without waiting.
- Queue file: a torn last line is cut back to the last newline under `LedgerLock` before any read or append; an unparseable line is kept, skipped and reported; rewrites go through a temporary file that replaces the queue.

## 5. Sharing (N4)

A share lock per clone (restored; v2 removed it and caused false rewrite refusals) serializes shares; a command that does not need the result skips the share if the lock is taken.

Under the share lock:

1. `git fetch` the default branch into a ref owned by this clone.
2. Rewrite check: if the last seen tip is not an ancestor of the fetched head, refuse: "the backlog history was rewritten; run basicly tracker fsck --repair". `fsck --repair` finds this writer's events at its last pushed commit (kept alive by a local tag), queues the missing ones, and accepts the new head.
3. Under `LedgerLock`, read the queue.
4. Drop queued events whose ids are anywhere on the fetched head, valid or void. If an id appears twice in the log, the fold keeps the first copy, so a crash can never bring a void claim back.
5. Build the commit with git plumbing: a temporary index from the fetched head, this writer's file with the queued events appended, `commit-tree` with the fetched head as the only parent.
6. `git push <commit>:<default branch>`, plain. On success, write the last seen tip and the local tag, and under `LedgerLock` remove the shared events from the queue by id.
7. Drain bound: a share sends the events queued when it started, then makes one more pass for events written meanwhile, then stops. The last check of the queue and the release of the share lock happen while `LedgerLock` is held, and every command that appends retries the share lock after its append, so the last writer always shares its own event and no sharer runs forever. The share lock is an operating-system lock like `LedgerLock`, released when its process dies.
8. On refusal, go to 1; after 5 attempts with random back-off the events stay queued, and each command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share" once, at the end.

Verified on local bare repositories (basicly-gtb19bg.58): this share kept 300 of 300 appends with no duplicates against concurrent pushers; a rebase-based share lost appends.

## 6. Reading and holder verdicts

- The tool only pushes commits whose single parent is the fetched head, so the branch is a straight line. The read layer walks it from the last cached commit; a commit with more than one parent (a merge pushed by plain git), a deleted or renamed writer file and a changed line are void; `fsck --repair` gives this writer's structurally void events (a merge, a rename, a changed line, a rewrite) new ids and queues them. It never re-queues an event that the holder rule voided, so a refused claim cannot come back.
- Lines that do not parse, lines changed after they were added and lines in a file whose header names another writer are void and reported.
- The fold gets an ordered mode for backlog ledgers: input order kept, duplicate ids dropped, equal `seq` values not a fork; `seq` and totals computed from the order; for an id that appears twice, the first copy counts.
- Holder verdict for every event that changes the holder, not only claims: a claim when the record is held by another session is void; an `unassign` is valid only from the holder or with `--take`; a take is valid and logged. The fold skips the field handler for a void event, so a void event never writes the holder. (Today `unassign` checks nothing, basicly-qtmesvv.)
- One conflict model: in the ordered mode the holder verdicts replace the `contested` state (`events.py:609-611`), the fork findings of `forks.py` and the `resolve` command (`arguments.py:243`); on a backlog ledger `resolve` refuses by name, because nothing is left to resolve.
- Migrated holders that are person names stay as legacy holders. An `unassign` is valid when the display name of the writer equals the legacy name; a claim by any session on such a record is void until that unassign or a take.

## 7. Claims

- Before a claim appends anything, the tool checks that the forge answers (`git ls-remote`, 5 s). Offline, it refuses and queues nothing.
- `claim <id>` shares at once and waits, 30 s, killing any running git process at the deadline. Exit codes: 0 claimed by this session; 3 held by another session ("held by <name> since <time>; run basicly tracker claim <id> --take if the holder is gone"); 4 pending, also when `--wait` runs out of time ("run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait"); 5 offline; 7 already held by this session (a second claim from the same session, for example from a subagent, does not count as a new claim).
- A pending claim that lands later is reported by the next command of the same session; release with `basicly tracker unassign <id>`.
- Measured on local repositories with 8 agents: every claim within 4.1 s at 1 s latency; a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency gave a 26 s median with pending results. Contention is the main open risk (section 15).

## 8. Closing a record from the code (N3)

- Where a close comes from (owner decision): only the subject of a commit on the first-parent chain of the code default branch. For a pull request that is the squash commit, whose subject is the pull request title; for a direct push it is that commit's subject. Message bodies and the commits inside a pull request are never read for status. This removes, as a class, the squash-body, revert-text and line-order defects of versions 3 to 5.
- Merge method: squash merges only, with the pull request title as the commit subject. On GitHub the kit's setup names the repository settings (allow squash merge only; default squash commit title is the pull request title); the PR check reads them through the API and refuses while they differ. On Bitbucket, whose squash default is not documented, `fsck --code` reports every first-parent commit whose subject does not match a merged pull request title, until the sandbox test settles it.
- Declarations in a subject: `closes <id>` closes; `reopens <id>` reopens; a record id at the end of the subject (`refs`, as the hooks require today) only links; `none` marks work with no record. A subject that holds both `closes` and `reopens` for one id is refused. One parser, built on the existing id regex (`claims.py:31`, `:53-58`), used by the hook, the PR check and the derivation; it refuses close-like words that are not exactly `closes` (`close`, `fixes`, `resolves`, `Closes`) by name.
- Reverts: declarations inside a quoted `Revert "..."` are ignored. A forge Revert button produces a title `Revert "<old title>"`; when the quoted old title holds `closes <id>`, the PR check requires `reopens <id>` outside the quotes and refuses `none` by name.
- Status rule, in the read layer: if a record has an effective code declaration on the fetched default branch of the code repository, its status is the latest code effect and backlog status events for it are ignored; otherwise its status is the latest backlog status event. A backlog close or reopen of a code-owned record is refused at write time with "this record closes from code: put reopens <id> or closes <id> in a pull request title". A record whose only code declaration was later cancelled stays code-owned.
- Who may close: anyone whose pull request is merged; the merge is the authorization, the same trust as the code itself. `fsck --code` lists every close with its commit. Named risk, deferred hardening: a maintainer merges a fork PR with an unread title.
- Links: any record id anywhere in any commit message reachable from the default branch links that commit to the record; links never change status.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: checks the declaration syntax of the commit subject and refuses an unknown id; it no longer requires a declaration in every commit, because only the pull request title counts. In contributor mode it checks syntax only. When `tracker.toml` exists and no clone does, it refuses with "run basicly tracker attach <url>" (or `--contributor`). Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m). The hook block carries a version marker; every command and the session start refuse a stale block and name `basicly tracker install-hook`.
- The old hook block runs only while `.basicly/ledger` exists (`claim_block.py:57`), so after cutover it checks nothing. Therefore the new hook block ships in a release before cutover and works with the in-repo ledger too. Each session start with the new release appends a hook-version event to the in-repo ledger, so the cutover can see who has it (section 11). A machine that skipped it is caught by the PR check and by `fsck --code`.
- PR check (CI template): extracts the kit from the PR's base commit and runs that copy. It requires a declaration in the PR title (section 8) and the squash-only settings; refuses a PR that changes `.basicly/ledger` once the base commit holds the freeze marker or after cutover; refuses a missing README line; refuses any change to the backlog URL in `tracker.toml` (moving a backlog is deferred); refuses a deletion of `tracker.toml` mixed with other changes. It never runs code from the PR. It runs on `pull_request` and passes values through environment variables. Whether a PR can weaken the check by editing the workflow file itself is a forge fact to settle on the sandbox; until then the workflow file is protected by the required-check setting and removed only in its own later PR (section 13).
- Required status check: the owner marks the PR check required at cutover. Enforcement depends on the plan: GitHub enforces it for public repositories on GitHub Free and for all repositories on Pro, Team and Enterprise; Bitbucket only warns without Premium (vendor docs). Where it is not enforced, the PR check advises and `fsck --code` at every session start reports every merge that bypassed a refusal. The kit states this guarantee per plan.
- `fsck --code` runs incrementally inside session start and every tracker command, from the last checked code commit, and prints each new void declaration with its next action. No credential is needed. A scheduled audit is deferred.
- `git_runner.py` validates values before git sees them (commit ids against `^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$`, writer ids against a fixed pattern, URLs against `https://` and `ssh://`, `file://` in tests), puts `--end-of-options` before values and allows only those protocols. Event text is stripped of control characters before a terminal or agent sees it.

## 10. Readable view (optional)

The board and CLI views read the machine clone; event lines are JSON with the record id and status in plain text; a team may add the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template.

## 11. Migration and cutover

0. Before cutover: the release with the new hook block is installed. `migrate --freeze` lists every writer that wrote to the in-repo ledger in the last 30 days without a hook-version event, and refuses unless the owner passes `--accept-missing` with those names.
1. `migrate --freeze` commits a marker into the old ledger, naming who froze it and when; from then on every in-repo write that sees the marker refuses with "the tracker is moving to a backlog; wait for the cutover, or run basicly tracker migrate --unfreeze", and the PR check refuses ledger changes on any PR whose base holds the marker. A branch cut before the freeze therefore cannot merge ledger writes. `migrate --unfreeze` removes the marker by commit if the cutover is abandoned; a later freeze and import resume by event id.
2. `migrate --to-backlog` imports the frozen ledger into an empty backlog as the migration writer, in today's fold order, keyed by event id; it resumes after a crash by skipping ids already imported, and refuses if any writer file other than its own exists. Nobody attaches before the cutover merges, so no other writer file can exist. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
3. `migrate --verify` writes a digest of the frozen ledger and the backlog head into `tracker.toml`; the cutover PR adds that file and the README line and deletes `.basicly/ledger`. The PR check compares the digest with the frozen ledger in the base commit; on a mismatch it names `migrate --to-backlog` then `migrate --verify`, which can always run again because the ledger is frozen.
4. Owner step: mark the PR check as a required status check where the plan allows.
5. After cutover, a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` is refused with `migrate --to-backlog --branch`, which imports the branch's comments and notes, lists its state changes for a person to re-enter, and then deletes the branch's ledger changes in one commit on that branch, so the PR passes. A revert of the cutover is refused; the undo is a forward PR.
6. Every in-repo ledger command refuses when `tracker.toml` exists: "the tracker moved to <url>; run the command without the ledger directory".

## 12. Changes and build order

- New in the kit (about 8): `git_runner.py`; attach, clone and queue; the share step; the ordered read layer; the declarations parser; the code-history derivation; claim exit codes and `--wait`; the PR check template.
- Replaced (4): the hook block, `commit-check` (`cli.py:254-282`), `locate.py`, the ledger part of `install_hook.py`.
- Changed: `events.py` (ordered mode, holder verdicts), `fsck.py`, `migrate.py` (freeze, import, verify), the 28 `directory` arguments. Replaced on backlog ledgers: the `contested` state, the fork findings of `forks.py` and the `resolve` command, which refuses by name.
- Outside the kit: 60 files and 168 lines in `src`, `tests` and `.basicly/core/hooks` name `.basicly/ledger`; one storage resolver in the kit serves them all. Guidance and skills change with the release.
- Build order, each slice behind `tracker.toml` so the in-repo ledger keeps working: S1 `git_runner.py` and the gate exemption; S2 ordered fold and holder verdicts (also fixes basicly-qtmesvv for today's ledger); S3 attach, queue, share, read layer (riskiest: a contention probe on a sandbox forge first); S4 claims; S5 parser and `fsck --code`, read-only and useful on today's ledger; S6 hook and PR check; S7 migration, cutover, resolver sweep, sandbox proofs.

## 13. Removal

In this order: the owner removes the required status check; `detach` on each machine shares the queue, appends a detached event and removes the hook block (if the share fails, it refuses and names `detach --export <file>`, which writes the queue to a file); one code PR deletes exactly `tracker.toml` and the README line; a second PR deletes the PR check workflow; the owner archives or deletes the backlog repository. `basicly tracker remove` lists every writer from the `log/` headers with its last event and detached state, and prints the archive step only when no writer with queued events is still attached.

## 14. Proof tests

On local bare repositories in CI, except where named:

- N1: 1000 tracker writes leave `git status --porcelain` empty in the code repository; on sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories at release, two code PRs that ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees write 1000 events against a remote with 1 s push latency; every event lands once; no `LedgerLock` wait above 1 s; two sessions share at once with no false rewrite refusal; a kill after the push and before the queue clear causes no duplicate; a torn queue tail is repaired; a copied clone gets a new writer id.
- N3: on the code default branch, a squash whose title says `closes <id>` closes; `reopens <id>` reopens; a `refs` id or an id in a message body changes nothing; a title with both `closes` and `reopens` for one id is refused; a Revert-button title quoting `closes <id>` is refused until it adds `reopens <id>`; `fixes <id>` is refused; a merge commit or a rebase merge is reported by `fsck --code`; a backlog close of a code-owned record is refused, and a stale writer's backlog close is ignored by the read rule. Locally with `git merge --squash` and a set subject; on the sandbox forges with each squash setting.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones and 8 sessions in one clone claim one record and exactly one session gets exit 0; an `unassign` by a non-holder is void; a claim pushed by plain git as a merge is void and `fsck --repair` restores its events; a pending claim resolves to one holder; a void claim re-sent after a crash stays void; an event written while the share lock was busy is shared before the lock is released; a force-push makes shares refuse and `fsck --repair` restores this writer's events; an offline claim queues nothing; a second claim from the same session returns exit 7; a sharer under a nonstop appender returns after one extra pass; a claim voided by the holder rule is not re-queued by `fsck --repair`.
- Migration: killed at each step it resumes to equal records; an in-repo write after `migrate --freeze` is refused; a PR from a branch cut before the freeze that changes the ledger is refused; freeze, unfreeze, write, freeze and import give equal records; freeze refuses while an active writer lacks the hook-version event; a digest mismatch is repaired by running import and verify again; a legacy name holder is released by an `unassign` from that name; an in-repo command after cutover refuses by name; `--branch` leaves the branch mergeable.
- Removal: a PR that deletes `tracker.toml` together with other files is refused; `detach` with an unsharable queue refuses and `--export` writes it; `remove` withholds the archive step while a writer with queued events is attached; a PR that changes the backlog URL is refused.
- Security: hostile values are refused by `git_runner.py`; the hook installed under a path with a double quote and `$(x)` runs nothing.

## 15. Deferred, open, owner actions

- Deferred (owner decision b): identity binding (author checks, signing), CODEOWNERS, `attach --restore` beyond `fsck --repair`, claim expiry, the backlog pre-push hook, the scheduled audit, one backlog for several code repositories, a required `BACKLOG.md`. Named risk: a fork PR merged unread can close a record.
- Deferred as well: moving a backlog to a new URL.
- Open: contention on a real forge (fallback: comments and fields on one branch per writer, claims and closes on the default branch); Bitbucket's squash default (not documented); whether `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` reaches the Bash commands of subagents (vendor docs say subagents share the session; to test before S4).
- Owner actions: approve the kit rule change (section 1); approve sandbox repositories on GitHub and Bitbucket with a scoped token as a CI secret; mark the PR check required at cutover where the plan allows.

## 16. Changes from version 4

| Round 3 blocker | Answer in version 5 |
| --- | --- |
| Reverts matched by commit id | No revert inference; a revert carries `reopens <id>`; both in one commit cancel (section 8) |
| `refs` reopens a backlog-closed record | `refs` never changes status; source rule keyed on a code close (section 8) |
| Stranded event, void claim re-pushed | Share loops until the queue is empty; ids anywhere on the head are dropped; first copy wins (section 5) |
| Legacy hold, digest mismatch | Unassign by the legacy name; `migrate --freeze` before import (sections 6, 11) |
| Removal bypass, URL change | Exact removal set; URL change refused; removal order (sections 9, 13) |
| Old hook after cutover | New hook ships and installs before cutover (sections 9, 11) |
| Two conflict models | Holder verdicts replace contested, forks and resolve (sections 6, 12) |
| Session identity | `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, or ids minted by `session new` (section 3) |
| Required check per plan | Guarantee stated per plan; `fsck --code` reports bypasses (section 9) |

## 17. Changes from version 5

| Open after the check of version 5 | Answer in version 6 |
| --- | --- |
| Close, revert, close in one squash; revert-only squash; Revert button with `none` | Status only from first-parent subjects (the PR title); squash only; quoted revert of a close needs `reopens` (section 8) |
| Parallel subagents share one session id | One session is one holder; exit 7 for a repeat claim (sections 3, 7) |
| Nobody sees whether every machine has the new hook | Hook-version event; freeze lists writers without it (sections 9, 11) |
| Pre-freeze branches, freeze without undo | PR check refuses ledger changes on a frozen base; `migrate --unfreeze` (section 11) |
| Unbounded share loop | One extra pass; last check and release under `LedgerLock` (section 5) |
| Repair brings back a refused claim | Repair re-queues only structurally void events (section 6) |
| Half-done removal, workflow edited by its own PR | Detached events, `--export`, ordered PRs (sections 9, 13) |
| Stale backlog close after a code reopen | Read rule: code-owned records follow code only (section 8) |

payload.text: [check of v6 2026-11-11, 3 Opus lenses] Resolved of the 8 rows in section 17: correctness 6, misuse 7, recovery 6. Confirmed: git merge --squash with a set message gives exactly that subject and one parent (git 2.55.0). Open, code close from titles: a revert of a revert cannot be declared (nested Revert, git Reapply subject); a quote inside the old title ends the quoted part early (ran); a title edited after the check or a squash subject edited at merge reaches main unchecked; a hand-written revert title escapes the reopens rule; closes only in a body is dropped silently; a merge method re-enabled after setup lets inner subjects close records. Open elsewhere: the share bound contradicts the skip rule and can strand an event (two lenses); unfreeze after a partial import cannot reach equal records and is offered to every writer; hook-version events block pre-freeze branches until cutover; an exported queue has no way back; removal order is printed, not refused.
