6. `git push <commit>:<default branch>`, plain. On success, write the last seen tip and the local tag, and under `LedgerLock` remove the shared events from the queue by id.
7. Drain bound: a share sends the events queued when it started, then makes one more pass for events written meanwhile, then stops. The last check of the queue and the release of the share lock happen while `LedgerLock` is held, and every command that appends retries the share lock after its append, so the last writer always shares its own event and no sharer runs forever. The share lock is an operating-system lock like `LedgerLock`, released when its process dies.
8. On refusal, go to 1; after 5 attempts with random back-off the events stay queued, and each command prints "not shared: N events queued since <time>; run basicly tracker share" once, at the end.

Verified on local bare repositories (basicly-gtb19bg.58): this share kept 300 of 300 appends with no duplicates against concurrent pushers; a rebase-based share lost appends.

## 6. Reading and holder verdicts

- The tool only pushes commits whose single parent is the fetched head, so the branch is a straight line. The read layer walks it from the last cached commit; a commit with more than one parent (a merge pushed by plain git), a deleted or renamed writer file and a changed line are void; `fsck --repair` gives this writer's structurally void events (a merge, a rename, a changed line, a rewrite) new ids and queues them. It never re-queues an event that the holder rule voided, so a refused claim cannot come back.
- Lines that do not parse, lines changed after they were added and lines in a file whose header names another writer are void and reported.
- The fold gets an ordered mode for backlog ledgers: input order kept, duplicate ids dropped, equal `seq` values not a fork; `seq` and totals computed from the order; for an id that appears twice, the first copy counts.
- Holder verdict for every event that changes the holder, not only claims: a claim when the record is held by another session is void; an `unassign` is valid only from the holder or with `--take`; a take is valid and logged. The fold skips the field handler for a void event, so a void event never writes the holder. (Today `unassign` checks nothing, basicly-qtmesvv.)
- One conflict model: in the ordered mode the holder verdicts replace the `contested` state (`events.py:609-611`), the fork findings of `forks.py` and the `resolve` command (`arguments.py:243`); on a backlog ledger `resolve` refuses by name, because nothing is left to resolve.
- Migrated holders that are person names stay as legacy holders. An `unassign` is valid when the display name of the writer equals the legacy name; a claim by any session on such a record is void until that unassign or a take.

## 7. Claims

- Before a claim appends anything, the tool checks that the forge answers (`git ls-remote`, 5 s). Offline, it refuses and queues nothing.
- `claim <id>` shares at once and waits, 30 s, killing any running git process at the deadline. Exit codes: 0 claimed by this session; 3 held by another session ("held by <name> since <time>; run basicly tracker claim <id> --take if the holder is gone"); 4 pending, also when `--wait` runs out of time ("run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait"); 5 offline; 7 already held by this session (a second claim from the same session, for example from a subagent, does not count as a new claim).
- A pending claim that lands later is reported by the next command of the same session; release with `basicly tracker unassign <id>`.
- Measured on local repositories with 8 agents: every claim within 4.1 s at 1 s latency; a nonstop remote writer at 2 s latency gave a 26 s median with pending results. Contention is the main open risk (section 15).

## 8. Keeping status in step with the code (N3)

- Owner decision of 2026-11-11: a record's status changes only through a backlog event (`close`, `reopen`). Code never changes a status by itself. Versions 3 to 6 derived status from commit messages and then from pull request titles; every check found new edge cases (squash bodies, revert texts, nested reverts, quotes in titles, subjects edited at merge, merge methods changed after setup). A suggestion that a person confirms does not need a perfect parser: a wrong suggestion is harmless.
- Suggestions: `fsck --code` reads the first-parent chain of the code default branch from the cutover commit on. For each subject that names a record with `closes <id>` or `reopens <id>`, or that is a revert (`Revert "..."`, `Reapply "..."`, or a body line "This reverts commit <sha>") of a commit that named a record, it suggests the matching backlog event when the record's status differs: "<sha> <subject> suggests: basicly tracker close <id>". It runs incrementally in session start and every tracker command, so drift is shown within one command after a fetch.
- Confirm: `basicly tracker close <id> --from <sha>` and `reopen <id> --from <sha>` record the event with the commit as evidence; `fsck --code --dismiss <sha>` records that a suggestion was looked at and needs nothing. A suggestion stays listed until it is confirmed or dismissed, so drift is never silent (N3 becomes: every difference between code and tracker is shown with its fix).
- Links: any record id in any commit message reachable from the default branch links the commit to the record; links never change status.
- Who may close: any writer, in the backlog, with the holder verdicts of section 6. A close from a fork PR title is only a suggestion, so the fork risk of versions 4 to 6 is gone.
- What goes away: the declaration requirement on commits and titles, the squash-only rule, the revert rules, the source rule and the code-owned status rule. The parser stays only to make suggestions; it refuses nothing.

## 9. Checks

- Local commit hook: no declaration check. When `tracker.toml` exists and no clone does, it refuses with "run basicly tracker attach <url>" (or `--contributor`). Paths pass through environment variables, never shell text (fixes basicly-7b2t44m). The hook block carries a version marker; every command and the session start refuse a stale block and name `basicly tracker install-hook`. With no `tracker.toml` and a clone present, the hook and every command say "the tracker was removed; run basicly tracker detach".
- The old hook block runs only while `.basicly/ledger` exists (`claim_block.py:57`), so after cutover it checks nothing. Therefore the new hook block ships in a release before cutover and works with the in-repo ledger too. Each session start with the new release appends a hook-version event to the in-repo ledger, so the cutover can see who has it (section 11). A machine that skipped it is caught by the PR check and by `fsck --code`.
- PR check (CI template): extracts the kit from the PR's base commit and runs that copy. It refuses a PR that changes `.basicly/ledger` once the base holds the freeze marker or after cutover (naming `migrate --to-backlog --branch`, which also works between freeze and cutover); refuses a missing README line; refuses any change to the backlog URL in `tracker.toml`; refuses a deletion of `tracker.toml` mixed with other changes; refuses a PR that deletes its own workflow while the base still holds `tracker.toml`. It never runs code from the PR, runs on `pull_request` with the `edited` type, and passes values through environment variables.
- Required status check: the owner marks the PR check required at cutover. Enforcement depends on the plan: GitHub enforces it for public repositories on GitHub Free and for all repositories on Pro, Team and Enterprise; Bitbucket only warns without Premium (vendor docs). Where it is not enforced, the PR check advises and `fsck --code` at every session start reports every merge that bypassed a refusal. The kit states this guarantee per plan.
- `fsck --code` runs incrementally inside session start and every tracker command, from the last checked code commit, and prints each new void declaration with its next action. No credential is needed. A scheduled audit is deferred.
- `git_runner.py` validates values before git sees them (commit ids against `^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$`, writer ids against a fixed pattern, URLs against `https://` and `ssh://`, `file://` in tests), puts `--end-of-options` before values and allows only those protocols. Event text is stripped of control characters before a terminal or agent sees it.

## 10. Readable view (optional)

The board and CLI views read the machine clone; event lines are JSON with the record id and status in plain text; a team may add the `BACKLOG.md` workflow template.

## 11. Migration and cutover

0. Before cutover: the release with the new hook block is installed. `migrate --freeze` lists every writer that wrote to the in-repo ledger in the last 30 days without a hook-version event, and refuses unless the owner passes `--accept-missing` with those names.
1. `migrate --freeze` commits a marker into the old ledger, naming who froze it and when; from then on every in-repo write that sees the marker refuses with "the tracker is moving to a backlog (frozen by <name> at <time>); wait for the cutover", and the PR check refuses ledger changes on any PR whose base holds the marker. A branch cut before the freeze therefore cannot merge ledger writes. `migrate --unfreeze --abandon-cutover` removes the marker by commit if the cutover is abandoned; it refuses once `tracker.toml` is on the default branch, and a later import starts with a new migration writer into an empty backlog. Hook-version events are left out of the import.
2. `migrate --to-backlog` imports the frozen ledger into an empty backlog as the migration writer, in today's fold order, keyed by event id; it resumes after a crash by skipping ids already imported, and refuses if any writer file other than its own exists. Nobody attaches before the cutover merges, so no other writer file can exist. Acceptance: a fold of the old and the new log gives equal records.
3. `migrate --verify` writes a digest of the frozen ledger and the backlog head into `tracker.toml`; the cutover PR adds that file and the README line and deletes `.basicly/ledger`. The PR check compares the digest with the frozen ledger in the base commit; on a mismatch it names `migrate --to-backlog` then `migrate --verify`, which can always run again because the ledger is frozen.
4. Owner step: mark the PR check as a required status check where the plan allows.
5. After cutover, a PR that touches `.basicly/ledger` is refused with `migrate --to-backlog --branch`, which imports the branch's comments and notes, lists its state changes for a person to re-enter, and then deletes the branch's ledger changes in one commit on that branch, so the PR passes. A revert of the cutover is refused; the undo is a forward PR.
6. Every in-repo ledger command refuses when `tracker.toml` exists: "the tracker moved to <url>; run the command without the ledger directory".

## 12. Changes and build order

- New in the kit (about 8): `git_runner.py`; attach, clone and queue; the share step; the ordered read layer; the declarations parser; the code-history derivation; claim exit codes and `--wait`; the PR check template.
- Replaced (4): the hook block, `commit-check` (`cli.py:254-282`), `locate.py`, the ledger part of `install_hook.py`.
- Changed: `events.py` (ordered mode, holder verdicts), `fsck.py`, `migrate.py` (freeze, import, verify), the 28 `directory` arguments. Replaced on backlog ledgers: the `contested` state, the fork findings of `forks.py` and the `resolve` command, which refuses by name.
- Outside the kit: 60 files and 168 lines in `src`, `tests` and `.basicly/core/hooks` name `.basicly/ledger`; one storage resolver in the kit serves them all. Guidance and skills change with the release.
- Build order, each slice behind `tracker.toml` so the in-repo ledger keeps working: S1 `git_runner.py` and the gate exemption; S2 ordered fold and holder verdicts (also fixes basicly-qtmesvv for today's ledger); S3 attach, queue, share, read layer (riskiest: a contention probe on a sandbox forge first); S4 claims; S5 parser and `fsck --code`, read-only and useful on today's ledger; S6 hook and PR check; S7 migration, cutover, resolver sweep, sandbox proofs.

## 13. Removal

In this order: the owner removes the required status check; `detach` on each machine shares the queue, appends a detached event and removes the hook block (if the share fails, it refuses and names `detach --export <file>`, which writes the queue to a file); one code PR deletes exactly `tracker.toml` and the README line; a second PR deletes the PR check workflow; the owner archives or deletes the backlog repository. `basicly tracker remove` lists every writer from the `log/` headers with its last event and detached state, and prints the archive step only when no writer with queued events is still attached.

## 14. Proof tests

On local bare repositories in CI, except where named:

- N1: 1000 tracker writes leave `git status --porcelain` empty in the code repository; on sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories at release, two code PRs that ran tracker writes stay mergeable after the first merges.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees write 1000 events against a remote with 1 s push latency; every event lands once; no `LedgerLock` wait above 1 s; two sessions share at once with no false rewrite refusal; a kill after the push and before the queue clear causes no duplicate; a torn queue tail is repaired; a copied clone gets a new writer id.
- N3: a squash titled `closes <id>` produces one suggestion within one command after a fetch; confirming it closes the record with the commit as evidence; a revert, a revert of a revert, a `Reapply`, a title with a quote inside it and a subject edited at merge each produce the suggestion that matches the final code, or none; a suggestion stays listed until confirmed or dismissed; a commit never changes a status by itself.
- N4: a comment on clone 1 is visible on clone 2 after one fetch; three clones and 8 sessions in one clone claim one record and exactly one session gets exit 0; an `unassign` by a non-holder is void; a claim pushed by plain git as a merge is void and `fsck --repair` restores its events; a pending claim resolves to one holder; a void claim re-sent after a crash stays void; an event written while the share lock was busy is shared before the lock is released; a force-push makes shares refuse and `fsck --repair` restores this writer's events; an offline claim queues nothing; a second claim from the same session returns exit 7; a sharer under a nonstop appender returns after one extra pass; a claim voided by the holder rule is not re-queued by `fsck --repair`.
- Migration: killed at each step it resumes to equal records; an in-repo write after `migrate --freeze` is refused; a PR from a branch cut before the freeze that changes the ledger is refused; freeze, unfreeze, write, freeze and import give equal records; freeze refuses while an active writer lacks the hook-version event; a digest mismatch is repaired by running import and verify again; a legacy name holder is released by an `unassign` from that name; an in-repo command after cutover refuses by name; `--branch` leaves the branch mergeable.
- Removal: a PR that deletes `tracker.toml` together with other files is refused; `detach` with an unsharable queue refuses and `--export` writes it; `remove` withholds the archive step while a writer with queued events is attached; a PR that changes the backlog URL is refused.
- Security: hostile values are refused by `git_runner.py`; the hook installed under a path with a double quote and `$(x)` runs nothing.

## 15. Deferred, open, owner actions

- Deferred (owner decision b): identity binding (author checks, signing), CODEOWNERS, `attach --restore` beyond `fsck --repair`, claim expiry, the backlog pre-push hook, the scheduled audit, one backlog for several code repositories, a required `BACKLOG.md`. Named risk: a fork PR merged unread can close a record.
- Deferred as well: moving a backlog to a new URL.
- Open: contention on a real forge (fallback: comments and fields on one branch per writer, claims and closes on the default branch); Bitbucket's squash default (not documented); whether `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` reaches the Bash commands of subagents (vendor docs say subagents share the session; to test before S4).
- Owner actions: approve the kit rule change (section 1); approve sandbox repositories on GitHub and Bitbucket with a scoped token as a CI secret; mark the PR check required at cutover where the plan allows.

## 16. Changes from version 4

| Round 3 blocker | Answer in version 5 |
| --- | --- |
| Reverts matched by commit id | No revert inference; a revert carries `reopens <id>`; both in one commit cancel (section 8) |
| `refs` reopens a backlog-closed record | `refs` never changes status; source rule keyed on a code close (section 8) |
| Stranded event, void claim re-pushed | Share loops until the queue is empty; ids anywhere on the head are dropped; first copy wins (section 5) |
| Legacy hold, digest mismatch | Unassign by the legacy name; `migrate --freeze` before import (sections 6, 11) |
| Removal bypass, URL change | Exact removal set; URL change refused; removal order (sections 9, 13) |
| Old hook after cutover | New hook ships and installs before cutover (sections 9, 11) |
| Two conflict models | Holder verdicts replace contested, forks and resolve (sections 6, 12) |
| Session identity | `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, or ids minted by `session new` (section 3) |
| Required check per plan | Guarantee stated per plan; `fsck --code` reports bypasses (section 9) |

## 17. Changes from version 5

| Open after the check of version 5 | Answer in version 6 |
| --- | --- |
| Close, revert, close in one squash; revert-only squash; Revert button with `none` | Status only from first-parent subjects (the PR title); squash only; quoted revert of a close needs `reopens` (section 8) |
| Parallel subagents share one session id | One session is one holder; exit 7 for a repeat claim (sections 3, 7) |
| Nobody sees whether every machine has the new hook | Hook-version event; freeze lists writers without it (sections 9, 11) |
| Pre-freeze branches, freeze without undo | PR check refuses ledger changes on a frozen base; `migrate --unfreeze` (section 11) |
| Unbounded share loop | One extra pass; last check and release under `LedgerLock` (section 5) |
| Repair brings back a refused claim | Repair re-queues only structurally void events (section 6) |
| Half-done removal, workflow edited by its own PR | Detached events, `--export`, ordered PRs (sections 9, 13) |
| Stale backlog close after a code reopen | Read rule: code-owned records follow code only (section 8) |

## 18. Changes from version 6

| Open after the check of version 6 | Answer in version 7 |
| --- | --- |
| Title rule edge cases (nested reverts, quotes, edited subjects, merge methods) | Code only suggests; a person or agent confirms (section 8) |
| Share bound contradicts the skip rule | Fixed in slice S3: an appender waits for the share lock, bounded, and shares its own event if still queued; the "not shared" notice is keyed to queue age |
| Unfreeze after a partial import; unfreeze offered to everyone | Unfreeze needs `--abandon-cutover`, refuses once `tracker.toml` is on the default branch, and starts a new migration writer |
| Hook-version events block pre-freeze branches | They are left out of the import, and the PR check ignores a change made only of them |
| Exported queue has no way back | `basicly tracker share --from <file>` re-queues with the original ids |
| Removal order only printed | The PR check refuses a PR deleting its own workflow while `tracker.toml` exists; commands name `detach` after removal |

Shared reasoning context removes repeated onboarding and lossy handoffs while preserving deterministic control.

payload.description:
## Context

The worktree concurrency cap counts recorded **sessions**, not directories. Two ways a session outlives
its directory were both hit on 2026-08-20:

- `basicly worktree cleanup` without `--force` removes the directory and keeps the session, so the slot
  stays held while `worktree list` marks it `(stale: dir missing)`.
- `git worktree remove` leaves the session entirely, because nothing tells the engine.

The result was `worktree concurrency cap reached (5/5)` with only three linked worktrees on disk, and
the error names the cap rather than the stale rows. An operator raises the cap instead of reclaiming a
slot, which is what happened.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `basicly worktree create a` and `git worktree remove` its directory.
2. Run `basicly worktree list` and observe `(stale: dir missing)`.
3. Create worktrees until the cap is reached.
4. Observe `worktree concurrency cap reached (N/N)` while fewer than N directories exist.
5. Observe the message names the cap and not the stale sessions holding the slots.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a session whose directory is gone when the cap is evaluated then it does not count toward the cap - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_worktree.py -k stale_slot -q`
- Given the cap is reached and stale sessions exist then the refusal names them and the command that reclaims them

## Scope

- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_worktree.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_worktree.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_worktree.py -k stale_slot -q`

payload.description:
## Context

The change-summary is the largest artifact population, 38 of 54, and what makes it large is `changed`, the changed-path list. The biggest recorded one is 18555 bytes of which 4096 is sorted paths and nothing else.

That list is already derivable from the commit the same artifact carries. Dropping it makes the artifact constant-size in the diff rather than linear, which is the correct bound: the decision on diff size already rules that a large diff is sometimes right, so refusing the artifact would refuse a correct landing for being correct about a large change.

This is the bound-by-derivability half of D-36. Where nothing is derivable, as with the release record, the body stays whole.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given a landing composes a change summary then the payload carries the commit, a changed-path count and a digest of the sorted list, and does not carry the list.
Given a reader needs the paths then it derives them from the commit.
Given a summary written before this change then the schema still accepts it.
Given a lane touching 400 files then the stored body is under 1000 bytes.
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_handoff.py tests/test_loop.py -q

## Scope

- `src/basicly/handoff.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `.basicly/core/schemas/change-summary.schema.json`
- `tests/test_handoff.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

payload.description:
Retro finding, session 2026-08-13. Proposed by the agent, not self-applied.

## Context

`module-size` counts tokens; `comment-density` counts the prose share. They can be
unsatisfiable together, and nothing in the catalog says so.

On `basicly-u2hl.54.3` the size ratchet forced 459 tokens out of `loop.py`. The honest
extraction available - the prompt builders - was **code**-heavy, so removing it raised the prose
share from 52.4% to 53.0% and broke the other gate. Six trim-and-remeasure cycles followed before
the pattern was named and the session stopped to ask the owner.

The rule that resolves it is arithmetic and cheap to state: **an extraction satisfies both gates
only if the extracted unit prose share is ABOVE the origin module share.** Extracting code raises
the origin share; extracting prose lowers it. The second extraction attempted that session - the
answered-escalation reader, at a higher prose share than `loop.py` - satisfied both in one pass.

The skill already carries the right stance ("Fix the metric, do not move the score", and the test
of stating what you did without naming the gate). What it lacks is the measurement that tells you
WHICH cut to make, so an author obeying the stance still cycles.

A second consequence belongs with it: **a prose-heavy extraction cannot stand alone.** A new
module has no frozen baseline, so a 66% module fails the 50% cap the moment it is created. That is
where a `comment-density-waiver` is legitimate and scoped, rather than on the 2600-line module it
came out of - which is what `landing_gate.py` records as the tree first such waiver.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Take any module over both caps, e.g. `loop.py`.
- Extract a code-heavy block to satisfy `module-size`.
- Run `uv run python .scripts/check_comment_density.py` - the origin now fails, and the skill
  offers no guidance on which block to have cut instead.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/python-guidelines/skill.yaml`
payload.title: teach python guidelines that the two size ratchets pull opposite ways

payload.text:
[partly done 2026-08-22] basicly-03ykuf landed the economics half of this into the skill. python-guidelines now states that removing a unit raises the parent's prose share whenever the unit is prose-lighter than the parent, that only 34.4 percent of 3588 real top-level definitions in the 68 frozen oversized modules are prose-heavier and so satisfy both gates, and that the bind applies to the 17 modules frozen in both tables rather than to every module.

What is NOT done and is what remains here: the guidance tells a lane to check the ratio and does not give it a way to compute it. A lane still has to write that measurement itself, which is most of what basicly-kr7t spent its budget on. Re-scope this onto the instrument rather than the prose - something that answers 'what does this cut do to both gates' before the cut is made, which is also basicly-e2r08j's ask from the gate side.

Do not re-add the prose; read the shipped skill first.

## Trigger
Item 7 of the Anthropic prompting audit (2026-09-12). The published guidance suggests a model should elicit requirements before starting. The audit flagged it to consider, not to adopt.

## Decision
Do not adopt. Recorded so the idea is not re-proposed without new evidence.

## Why
Three things already occupy the slot, and each is narrower and cheaper than a blanket intake step:

- `decision-protocol` already says to stop and ask when a fact cannot be found, sources conflict, or an unverifiable assumption would change the outcome. That is elicitation, gated on a condition.
- The harness loop has `needs-input.json`, a block-do-not-guess protocol that stops the lane rather than guessing.
- The owner has corrected the opposite behaviour more than once: propose with a recommendation rather than poll, and do not present options just to look thorough.

A blanket elicitation step would fire on every task including the ones with no ambiguity, which is the failure mode the existing rules were written to avoid.

## What would reopen this
Evidence that work is being started on a wrong reading often enough to pay for the questions. The gate-failure ledger is where that would show.

payload.description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 3. `basicly status --json` is single-repo and self-labelled (STATUS_SCHEMA_VERSION) "for fleet loops", and every dispatch drops a run-record into `.basicly/usage/`, but basicly does no aggregation across the housed repos of the dev workspace.

Add a read-only fleet rollup: `basicly status --fleet [--root PATH]` discovers the basicly-installed repos under the workspace root and rolls up, per repo, the `status --json` snapshot plus a run-record summary into one JSON payload. JSON-first, read-only, exit 0.

Rollup model (decided): in-process — call the current engine's `_status_report(repo_root)` on each discovered repo plus `run_record.load_run_records`; a per-repo failure is captured as an `error` field, never failing the whole rollup. Default root is the parent of the current repo; `--root` overrides. Reuses the existing single-repo status + run-record loaders (no new snapshot logic).

## Acceptance Criteria

- `basicly status --fleet` discovers the basicly repos (immediate subdirs of the workspace root containing a `.basicly/` dir), and emits a JSON payload `{schema_version, workspace_root, repos: [...], totals: {...}}`, sorted deterministically by repo name, exit 0.
- Each repo entry carries its name, the `status --json` payload (or an `error` string if the snapshot raises), and a run-record summary (total runs, counts by outcome, distinct agents/models, beads with runs).
- The command writes nothing anywhere (read-only) and returns 0 even when a repo is unreadable, has no `.basicly/`, or has no run-records.
- `--root PATH` overrides the discovered workspace root; the default is the parent of the current repo.
- Totals aggregate the per-repo run-record counts across the fleet.
- Full suite, ruff, ruff format, pyright, bandit, and the projection gates (basicly check / skills-check / agents-check / hooks-check) pass; verified by exercising the real command against this workspace (not just unit tests).

## Notes

- Cross-repo scope is READ-ONLY aggregation only (dimension 3's explicit ask); it respects the workspace boundary (no writes, no cross-repo mutation, no --add-dir).
- Human-formatted fleet table and a subprocess-per-repo execution model are out of scope (JSON-first, in-process).
payload.title: Observability: fleet rollup across housed repos

payload.description:
## Trigger

When one engine process reads tracker kits from different checkouts or across an in-place update, I want each module graph to match its requested source revision, so I can finish landing without mixing incompatible APIs.

## Steps to Reproduce

In scratch archives of the generation repair parent and candidate e853cf06, load old events with owned_store.kit, then request new events. The same old module is returned. First-load new recurrence and resolve a gate draft. The new recurrence calls generation_bounds on old events and raises AttributeError. Also reproduced after loading old events then replacing that same scratch kit directory with the new source before loading recurrence. The release landing merged successfully before its verification write hit this error. A fresh native loop reran the required checks, recognized the already-landed branch, recorded verification and shipped successfully.

## Cause

The engine cache key includes the directory, but its sys.modules lookup uses one global name for every tracker module. Kit sibling loaders use those same global names. Source-path comparison alone cannot handle an in-place revision change or retained modules with lazy sibling loads.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/owned_store.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/*.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/SPEC.md`
- `tests/test_owned_store.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_kit_loading.py`

## Release Decision

Deferred from v0.26.12 because correct graph isolation needs a separate source-revision contract. Native recovery completed without manual tracker writes or bypassed gates. Specialist searched 1749 folded records and comments with the generation repair as positive control, found seven related loader/cache records, and found no exact open owner. The broad basicly-c25o52c is related context.
payload.requirements: Keep engine and standalone tracker loading compatible. Cover source namespaces, revision validity, lazy imports and failure rollback. Preserve all verification and ledger gates. Do not rely only on global eviction or top-level source-path comparison.
payload.title: Keep tracker module graphs tied to their kit source revision

Observed live while re-recording the tutorial against a 0.12.0 engine. The hook's own contract already makes an unreachable engine advisory, so an unresolvable pin now takes that path instead of blocking every commit.

payload.description:
Follow-up to basicly-c9e5 agreed with the user: (1) the loop engine commits tracker-only base dirt (claim, work type, classify approval) at worktree provisioning time - _start_build_leaf and _ensure_child_worktrees call commit_tracker_state before creating worktrees - so a teammate pulling the repo sees the claim in git history from the moment work starts instead of at landing; (2) the harness-loop skill replaces the flat push-once-per-track guidance with a solo/team nuance: solo batches pushes to end of track, a team repo pushes tracker commits as soon as the engine makes them (they are CI-free via paths-ignore) so claims propagate promptly. Cross-machine races that still slip through remain covered by br stale-claim detection (scheduler --stale-claim-hours, coordination).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Provisioning a leaf (and feature fan-out) commits pending tracker-only dirt first, with a conventional chore message referencing the issue; non-beads dirt does not block provisioning and is left alone (tests cover both). The harness-loop skill documents the three engine commit points (claim at provisioning, rollup at landing, close at ship) and the solo vs team push cadence. Full gate suite passes.
payload.title: Commit the claim at provisioning and document team push cadence

payload.description:
## Trigger

When harness work consumes hours and excessive inference, I want the complete audit and recommendations preserved in the tracker, so I can approve focused changes that reduce time and token waste.

## Findings and reasons

Repeated verification, compulsory tracker ceremony, broad context priming, conflicting repair and validation roles, consumer prompts referencing authoring-only scripts, whole-batch completion barriers, findings delivered only at redispatch, cleanup after closure and late confirmation are established mechanisms. Tracker UI polling adds repeated requests. Historical full verification took 185.826 seconds including pytest 138.127 seconds. A fresh ranking profile took 0.861 seconds wall and 0.806 seconds process CPU; this does not establish sustained saturation or hours-scale effects across consumer repositories.

## Durable evidence

The audit-report artifact contains every recommendation and reason, evidence citations, all 26 skill dispositions, 307 file dispositions and the conceptual dependency map. The audit-evidence artifact contains the tracked inventory, resolved dependencies and independent kit/web reviews. Static dependency references do not prove runtime reachability. Existing performance program basicly-c25o52c remains distinct.

## Approval boundary

User authorized this audit, tracker persistence and next-release planning on 2026-10-17. Filing a story is not implementation approval. All recommendations require individual review and approval. Do not claim, dispatch, implement, cut a release or change policy from this outline. Existing records, requirements, ownership and pre-existing ledger work must remain intact.

body.implementation: All recommendations pending individual user approval. AUD identifiers are proposed audit items, not tracker IDs.

observations.limits: Historical timings are wall time in this checkout. One profiled ranking invocation includes profiler overhead. No consumer-repository end-to-end or sustained CPU benchmark was run. No promised speedup.

recommendations.change: Remove automatic adjacent improvements and mandatory catalog-control work from ordinary repairs; allow a reproducible first defect to be fixed.
recommendations.reason: Local ownership and core completion rules broaden work; root-cause is injected for every bug but says stop after a first occurrence.
recommendations.title: Constrain work to the approved outcome

recommendations.change: Provide a small-task contract with intent, criteria, ownership and observed outcomes; avoid mandatory six-part rationales and synthetic same-card conversations.
recommendations.reason: Readiness/claim/close enforce ceremony in code; prompt compression alone cannot remove it.
recommendations.title: Make tracker evidence proportional

recommendations.change: Measure representative small fix, docs change, consumer install/upgrade and concurrent lanes using existing timing data first; set time/token budgets and collect CPU only where attribution is missing.
recommendations.reason: Existing measurements cover individual checks and dispatches; hours-to-minutes and CPU saturation are not established.
recommendations.title: Establish an end-to-end performance baseline

recommendations.change: Move the required completion confirmation check ahead of the first merge, retaining subsequent evidence checks.
recommendations.reason: Current normal path can merge and only then refuse confirmation.
recommendations.title: Confirm before merging

recommendations.change: Preserve owned work safely and make outstanding cleanup resumable before completion reads as done.
recommendations.reason: Current ship closes before cleanup, and closed derives done on resume.
recommendations.title: Make cleanup retryable

recommendations.change: Select release-note/headroom commands from capabilities the consumer actually has; keep authoring-only behavior in the authoring profile or package a generic implementation.
recommendations.reason: Universal dispatch references private .scripts/check_release_notes.py; shipped headroom hook also depends on private .scripts/headroom.py.
recommendations.title: Repair consumer versus authoring boundaries

recommendations.change: Share verification identity and valid evidence across CLI, hooks, rebased lane, merged tree and push where their actual inputs match; extend reuse check by check.
recommendations.reason: Full tests repeat; existing receipts/cache cover selected Pyright commands and are already enabled. Preserve staged-content and changed-input refusals.
recommendations.title: Avoid repeated equivalent verification

recommendations.change: Feed completed outcomes into the serial dependency-aware landing queue without waiting for the entire dispatch batch.
recommendations.reason: dispatch_lanes waits for all futures before CLI routes any result.
recommendations.title: Land completed lanes while others run

recommendations.change: Extend existing durable found-info routing with recipient scope, sequence and acknowledgement; start with the current coordination mechanism.
recommendations.reason: Findings currently arrive in later dispatch bundles, not running workers; a replacement messaging framework is unnecessary to address that gap.
recommendations.title: Deliver targeted findings to running lanes

recommendations.change: Check planned worktree/Git/protected output operations once and surface exact actionable mismatches; reuse existing write preflight and preserve scoped grants and dotenv denials.
recommendations.reason: Current Codex profiles exist; supervisor preflight does not prove these writes are authorized. PATH engine resolution can also disagree with installed kit version.
recommendations.title: Preflight effective permissions and runtime

recommendations.change: Replace mandatory whole architecture priming with a short current contract and relevant sections; shorten repeated orientation and redundant task instructions.
recommendations.reason: Architecture is 5646 lines; every non-trivial task is told to read it. Skill listings and injected bodies need separate budgets.
recommendations.title: Load context by task

recommendations.change: Choose review work by actual risk and useful repair evidence, report actual gate status, distinguish per-issue ship from release, and supply portable role instructions to Codex.
recommendations.reason: Reviews run serially after FAIL/undecodable verdict too; they intentionally aid repairs. Install versus read-only and push/ship wording conflict, and Codex lacks the resolved role body.
recommendations.title: Make validation and role contracts consistent

recommendations.change: Keep delivery essentials; make authoring, discovery, release, retention and vendor-audit tools optional. Correct zero-use pruning before removing any skill.
recommendations.reason: Skill-tool counters miss inline delivery and some host paths; absence of a recorded invocation is not proof a skill is useless.
recommendations.title: Offer lean skill profiles with reliable usage evidence

recommendations.change: Use measured CPU/I/O demand to admit concurrent check processes separately from agent process slots; use prepared lockfile-consistent dependencies.
recommendations.reason: Agent limits already exist; nominal pytest worker totals do not establish saturation. Worktree provisioning still copies node_modules and may npm install.
recommendations.title: Budget verification resources separately

recommendations.change: Prune excluded directories before traversal, share tracked-file/AST inputs within a check run, and measure headroom only for the requested file.
recommendations.reason: Comments CLI filters after rglob; multiple gates scan the same tree; pre-edit headroom measures all modules.
recommendations.title: Reduce script traversal work

recommendations.change: Pass one immutable folded/indexed view through write guards and revisions while retaining the ledger lock and invalidation rules.
recommendations.reason: A write reads the ledger through multiple guards and append; readiness repeatedly traverses events. Fresh ranking profile is sub-second, so do not present it as the principal hours-scale cause.
recommendations.title: Reuse a ledger view within each transaction

recommendations.change: Use change-triggered shared data and single-flight requests; preserve drafts/focus and back off when hidden.
recommendations.reason: A refresh issues nine API calls plus two for an open card; two-second version polling and unconditional fifteen-second reload overlap.
recommendations.title: Refresh tracker UI without repeated full loads

recommendations.change: Keep concise current contracts, move historical decisions/measurements and target designs out of compulsory priming, and reconcile contradictions and stale examples.
recommendations.reason: D25 conflicts with the absolute comment ban; decision index stops at D44 while body reaches D51; status and kit docs contain superseded claims despite structural doc gates.
recommendations.title: Separate current docs from historical designs

recommendations.change: Retain the standalone comments kit for users who choose it; stop imposing an absolute comment/docstring ban on every consumer by default.
recommendations.reason: It is house policy with unmeasured delivery benefit, conflicts with D25, and can create unrelated edits and documentation displacement. Keep safe-strip proofs if the kit remains enabled.
recommendations.title: Make the comment ban an explicit policy choice

recommendations.change: Remove the separate parentheses-style checker and its redundant guidance if approved; retain parser, lint, type and compatibility checks.
recommendations.reason: It spends a whole-tree tokenization pass enforcing house syntax style rather than a demonstrated defect class. Kit Python compatibility remains a separate requirement.
recommendations.title: Retire the except-form style gate

recommendations.change: Review wired-or-deleted overlap with vulture and filename-only test coverage; retain only controls tied to a demonstrated behavioral failure.
recommendations.reason: Unqualified names/string references and test filenames are weak evidence of real wiring or test coverage, while adding scans and maintenance. Retirement requires explicit policy approval.
recommendations.title: Replace duplicate heuristic wiring checks

recommendations.change: Keep Conventional Commits and the record link; remove arbitrary description character restrictions and universal word-count constraints where they add no consumer value.
recommendations.reason: Mechanical phrasing refusals consume repair turns without establishing correctness.
recommendations.title: Simplify incidental commit and prose rules

recommendations.change: Prepare one candidate artifact/environment and bind reusable proof to its exact inputs; remove redundant setup and checks while retaining fresh-install/upgrade/offline/foreign-hook evidence.
recommendations.reason: The release skill repeats checks and scratch setup; workflow builds artifacts in multiple jobs. The release path should reuse valid evidence instead of requiring repeated manual reconstruction.
recommendations.title: Reuse release preparation and consumer proof

body.scope: Read-only audit. Canonical sources reviewed for generated duplicates; 225 tracked Markdown paths, 26 skill bodies, 43 root Python scripts plus bootstrap/renderer, 28 hook Python files, all 59 kit Python modules and standalone package entry/helper scripts. Static graph inventory includes tests; not every test body was semantically reviewed. Non-script HTML/CSS/templates structurally scanned, not a visual audit. No dotenv reads, network, implementation, tracker writes or full test suite.
